articles.title_orig: CalChamber Backs Extending Suspension of China-Built Vessel Fees
articles.title_zh: CalChamber Backs Extending Suspension of China-Built Vessel Fees
articles.content_orig:
Last week the California Chamber of Commerce joined 250 trade associations in urging the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative (USTR) to support extending for two months the suspension of the fee on China-built vessels. The trade associations included importers, exporters, retailers, manufacturers, agriculture groups, logistics providers, and other users of the international freight transportation system. Their call for suspending the Section 301 China-built vessel fees came in an Oct. 30 letter to the USTR. The fee suspension was part of the Sept. 23 “Busan Agreement” trade truce, which had been scheduled to expire Nov. 10 and now is due to expire on Jan. 10, 2027. The overall extension was announced as Chinese President Xi Jinping met with President Donald Trump in Washington, D.C. in September 2026. But the USTR still needed to issue an official Federal Register notice, which is required to legally bind the fee postponement. The letter from the trade associations is part of this process, which closes on Nov. 10. The associations expect there will be a need to extend the fee suspension again before it ends in January.
In the letter, the associations express appreciation for the USTR’s efforts to address longstanding concerns about unfair practices affecting the maritime, logistics, and shipbuilding sectors. Strengthening U.S. maritime capacity and resilience is an important national objective. At the same time, the letter notes, imposing new or resumed fees on China-built or China-linked vessels would create immediate and far-reaching consequences for U.S. companies that rely on ocean transportation to move goods into and out of the United States. Resuming the Section 301 vessel fees in January 2027 would add another cost layer to an already-strained transportation, the letter asserts.
In spring 2024, at the request of the United Steelworkers and four other unions, the USTR opened an investigation under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, as a way to rebuild the U.S. shipbuilding industry. A January 2025 USTR 182-page report detailed the decline of U.S. shipbuilding and U.S. flag carriers, and highlighted the dramatic expansion of China’s shipbuilding and ship operating sectors due to massive subsidies and preferential treatment. Proposed remedies included significant “port service fees” against China-built ships every time they enter a U.S. port. The fee also would have applied to operators with China-built vessels in their fleet or having China-built vessels on order. The remedy further included a requirement for U.S. exporters to export a certain percentage of goods on vessels owned, operated and eventually built in the United States. The proposed remedies would have resulted in fees ranging from $1 million to $3 million — even as high as $3.5 million per port call. Reactions were mixed: Unions and steel makers were supportive of the remedies, while carriers, shippers and farm exporters were strongly opposed. A March 2025 study assessing the probable net economic effects of the proposed remedies found that overall, total exports and imports would decline, which would have a negative impact on the U.S. economy while the administration is trying to grow the overall economy and create jobs around the country. All agreed that China’s dominance of the shipping industry should be addressed as the United States has lost more than 70,000 jobs in the last few decades and now ranks 19th globally in shipbuilding. Further, while China builds more than 1,000 ocean vessels for commercial use per year, the United States produces fewer than 10. Originally the United States was to begin imposing new shipping fees in October 2025 that could have increased the cost of Chinese goods and potentially reduced imports. The Trump administration then agreed to pause the fees for a one-year period that would have ended Nov.10, 2026 before the latest extension to Jan. 10, 2027.

articles.title_orig: Beijing launches diplomatic flurry amid threat of renewed U.S. war with Iran
articles.title_zh: Beijing launches diplomatic flurry amid threat of renewed U.S. war with Iran
articles.content_orig:
Amid growing concerns about renewed attacks on Iran following Tuesday’s midterm elections in the United States, US forces have struck Iran’s Qeshm Island in what officials have reportedly described as a defensive measure.
In the first attack since June on Qeshm Island, which serves as the primary platform for Iran’s “asymmetric” naval power , according to analysts, the US strikes come as both sides continue to adopt military and diplomatic postures.
Mediation efforts led by Qatar are continuing in a bid to avert a return to all-out war, which began on February 28 when the US and Israel launched strikes across Iran, triggering the closure of the critical Strait of Hormuz, surging oil and gas prices and massive damage to military, civil and energy facilities around the Gulf.
Several explosions were heard on Qeshm Island late on Monday, as US media reported that the US military had carried out what officials called “defensive strikes” in the Strait of Hormuz.
The blasts came in rapid succession, according to Iran’s state-owned IRNA news agency. Witnesses told the agency they saw two planes flying over the island, located off Iran’s southern coast along the waterway.
According to The Wall Street Journal, which quoted an unnamed official, the strikes on Monday night appeared limited and were not a resumption of a major operation.
The Associated Press news agency also quoted an unnamed US official as saying Washington had conducted the defensive strikes against “Iranians using surface-to-air missiles against US assets”.
The attack came after IRNA reported that the Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) had destroyed a US MQ-9 drone east of the Strait of Hormuz.
The US first struck a critical desalination plant on Qeshm Island on March 7 – one week into the war. The strike, which Tehran branded a “flagrant crime” against civilians, cut off freshwater supplies to 30 surrounding villages.
It is, but it is fragile, and mixed messages are coming from both sides.
Qatari mediators have been engaged in indirect talks with Iranian officials in recent days. They have passed messages between the two sides, but the talks appeared to come to an end on Monday with no news of a breakthrough.
An official briefed on the talks told the Reuters news agency that Iran’s delegation had departed from Doha on Sunday, but that a draft proposal was still being circulated, without elaborating on the content.
Qatari mediators travelled to Tehran on Monday night for talks with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi regarding a version of a draft US-Iran deal which has been under negotiation for the past eight days, an official told Reuters.
Araghchi told IRNA on Monday: “Consultations through mediators are very intensive. We have presented our conditions and proposals, and everything depends on the political rationality of Washington.”
Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei also told a news conference on Monday that the “ball” was in the US’s court as Iran’s demands were “clear and logical”.
He said the plan Iran submitted in September to end the war remained the focus of talks, but that the proposal could be shortened and implemented in “two days”, including reopening the Strait of Hormuz and returning to talks about Iran’s nuclear programme.
On Monday, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian also said Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei had given the government “certain authorities” over talks with the US, local media reported.
The president added that Tehran would look to resolve the conflict through dialogue.
Khamenei’s apparent approval of diplomacy marks a change since the breakdown of the June memorandum of understanding , which allowed a brief ceasefire and peace negotiations, when the supreme leader said the US could not be trusted.
For the US side, Vice President JD Vance also told reporters on Monday that he was hopeful for a diplomatic solution – just hours before the strikes on Qeshm Island.
“The president and I both feel pretty good about the prospects for potentially coming to a negotiated settlement,” Vance said. “We’ve certainly made some progress. We’ll see if we can make some more.”
Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf reiterated on Tuesday that Iran’s response to any US “miscalculation”, such as launching strikes, would be unpredictable.
“The enemy seeks to force the Iranian nation into submission through threats and military action, but they are sorely mistaken; Iran will not submit,” he said.
Oil prices dropped by more than 7 percent on Monday. In response, Trump wrote on his Truth Social account that people believe the war with Iran will not resume as mediation efforts continue.
“Iran wants a settlement, as soon as possible. It could happen!” Trump wrote.
He told media at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool in Washington, DC, that it looked like efforts were “coming together very nicely”.
“That’s why I guess the oil prices dropped. People found out about it.”
However, Trump also told the US media outlet Axios before his post on Truth Social that he was “in no rush” to decide whether to resume strikes on Iran.
“One way or the other, we will do something, but there is no rush. We crippled them financially. They have no money, no gasoline, and their people are getting very tired of it,” Trump told Axios in an interview.
The US midterm elections are being viewed as the inflexion point for Trump’s decision on what path he takes next.
The president has suggested several times that he could attack Iran following the vote and told the Right Side Broadcasting Network (RSBN) on Sunday that the conflict would end “very soon one way or the other”, adding that Tehran would either “make a deal, or we’ll just end it”.
Observers say the US will likely renew strikes on Iran’s nuclear facilities if they do resume.
In particular, this could include Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain , a highly fortified site that contains two tunnel complexes buried deep underground, and which Trump told US outlet Newsmax last month could be a target. He said the US “may have to go there. We’ll take a shot at that one. We’ll knock it out fast.”

articles.title_orig: Google Will Turn Off Search for Schools That Reject A.I.
articles.title_zh: Google Will Turn Off Search for Schools That Reject A.I.
articles.content_orig:
Google announced it will "entirely" turn off Google Search, along with Gemini, Gemini Notebook, and Gemini in Classroom for K-12 schools. "Access to these products will be entirely off for K-12 student accounts until school administrators explicitly turn them on," Google wrote .
Google said it is doing this because "schools, teachers, leading researchers, and policymakers" asked them to.  Google wrote:
Google said it will "share more specifics with schools in the coming months ahead of the changes rolling out so they have time to prepare and enable a smooth transition."
"Our goal is simple: provide school leaders the control and confidence to use AI products in classrooms as they see fit," Google added.
Google also released a 29 page PDF on AI in Education .
Google is also releasing "Guided Learning capabilities into Search for student accounts to help them work through problems without skipping straight to answers."

articles.title_orig: Beyond screens: Mercedes-Benz’s new holographic heads-up display
articles.title_zh: Beyond screens: Mercedes-Benz’s new holographic heads-up display
articles.content_orig:
Do screens in cars represent luxury? Judging by the latest car interiors, the answer would seem to be an emphatic “yes.” Screens aren’t just getting larger; they are multiplying across the dashboard and morphing into different forms and concepts. Indeed, an interior’s screens are a pretty good indicator of what brand made the car—or at least how much the owner paid for it.
But is this actually what customers want ? Are more screens really better? And even if they are, luxury car features inevitably trickle down to cheaper, more mainstream offerings, and screens can only get so big. That leaves luxury automakers with another question to answer: “What’s next?”
Mercedes-Benz is working on a new display alternative that could provide an answer. For now, it’s known as the holographic display. Forget the images from Star Trek and Star Wars that just popped into your head, though. It’s effectively a more advanced form of heads-up display, or HUD.
Whereas a traditional HUD projects images onto the windshield glass, the holographic display has two main components. It still uses a projector, but its key element is a special transparent film laminated into the glass. The film uses holographic optical elements, or “super-small mirrors,” as Mercedes development engineer Lena Hees described them, that selectively reflect the light emitted by the projector, keeping the image visible even in direct sunlight while hiding it from the driver’s view.
Today, the passenger-side touchscreens in Mercedes and other luxury vehicles rely on driver-monitoring cameras or screen polarization to keep the driver from seeing what is playing on the passenger side.
Speaking of passenger screens, the holographic display is clearly being considered as a future alternative or replacement for this technology. Although screens in cars are increasingly ubiquitous, a recent JD Power study indicated that car owners classify passenger screens as “ not necessary ” and have generally negative opinions about them. Mercedes has clearly observed similar opinions but for slightly different reasons.
“We have customers who like the Hyperscreen,” said development engineer Maximilian Hilger of the pillar-to-pillar screen found in an increasing number of Mercedes models. “But there are others who want to maintain luxury materials.”
In other words, the massive screen design doesn’t seem as luxurious as the pillar-to-pillar bands of wood or other materials found in previous-generation models. And that’s not an opinion isolated to Mercedes’ customers.
New Mercedes chief design officer Bastian Baudy recently told German magazine Auto Motor Sport that “Materiality and haptics must remain tangible—with switches, buttons, and intuitive controls. Real materials are at the heart of Mercedes: metal, wood.”
Mercedes CEO Ola Källenius went further, grouping interior quality and materials among the brand’s “forever values,” along with safety and maintaining what a Mercedes is like to drive.
That presents conflicting priorities, however.
“Yes, you need to have all the [technology] that a customer could ever dream of and wants,” Källenius told Ars. “But you need to package it in an aesthetically pleasing way. That’s also part of it.”
That brings us back to the holographic display. Keep in mind that the photos in this article show early prototypes I saw at Mercedes’ research facilities in Sindelfingen, Germany. The prototype projector sits inside a rather crude, trapezoidal hole dug into the dash of a right-hand-drive, pre-2027 S-Class. It’s also loud, with a cooling fan whirring like a laptop visiting too many junk-filled websites.
The production version would have a much smaller projector opening than those of the prototype and existing heads-up displays. Manual Holstein, a manager working in Mercedes research for future displays, indicated that the projector could be small enough to be hidden behind wood or metal trim pieces. Holstein also said you won’t hear a fan in the production model and that the resolution would improve.
The resolution is certainly considerably better than any current head-up display, including Mercedes’ own, which features augmented reality elements . Full-color, commercial-like videos of the C-Class Electric played during the demonstration, and the display was sufficiently bright, even though Holstein said the prototype was operating at just 20 percent of its maximum brightness.
Issues remain, however. The resolution may be good compared to the arrows, script, and graphics of a current HUD, but it’s poor when compared to a passenger touchscreen. The video’s contrast was also too high, and as you can see in the photos, the picture was distorted into a narrow height due to the angle of the windshield. Frankly, no one would choose to watch anything on it over a phone, tablet, or conventional passenger screen. It needs to improve by orders of magnitude before becoming a viable alternative.
Again, though, this is just a prototype. Holstein said the holographic film size, or “eyebox,” can be made much bigger and be raised higher than the HUD-like height of the prototype. He also dismissed the distortion as a problem unique to the prototype.
Imagine nearly half the windshield transformed into a virtual screen that’s visible only to the passenger. Beyond videos or other entertainment, Mercedes envisions the holographic display highlighting points of interest in the view through the windshield. A similar display could be placed on the driver side, showing situational information, enabling video calls, or providing entertainment when parked. In the future, it could even let drivers watch things other than the road when Mercedes’ Level 3 autonomous driving system allows them to take their eyes off it. At the very least, the technology could replace today’s HUDs and their larger projector boxes.
Having experienced the prototype while the car was moving, I also think the holographic display could help prevent the motion sickness that can come from staring at a passenger screen while the car is moving. The higher screen angle and ability to see more of the outside world beyond created a notably different visual experience.
Of course, the question remains: “Is this what customers want?”
If the JD Power survey found that customers don’t care about passenger touchscreens, will they be any more enthusiastic about holographic video displays? That seems doubtful. But that’s just as much of an open question as whether the production version will actually live up to its promises.
There’s also another matter: What, exactly, defines luxury? Before Bastian Baudy took over as Mercedes’ chief design officer this year, his predecessor and former boss Gordon Wagener echoed Källenius’ thoughts about the direction of the brand’s interiors. He was considerably blunter, though.
“Screens are not luxury,” Wagener told ABC News . “You have a better—and bigger—TV at home, right? And every car has a big screen. So we have to create luxury beyond the screen. That’s why I talk about craftsmanship and sophistication.”
If the holographic display lets automakers emphasize traditional design and materials while still offering unique technology, it could be a promising way forward.

articles.title_orig: The 2026 iPad Mini is a terrific tiny tablet — for a big price
articles.title_zh: The 2026 iPad Mini is a terrific tiny tablet — for a big price
articles.content_orig:
With better performance and a better screen, this is a Mini to be reckoned with. But it’s not perfect, and it sure isn’t cheap.

The iPad Mini sometimes feels like a trap. It is, in some ways and for some people, the perfect iPad: meaningfully larger than my phone’s screen but still small and light enough to use for reading in bed or gaming on the subway. As most of the rest of the iPad line has tilted ever closer to laptop territory, the Mini might be the most iPad-y iPad left. I’ve taken a Mini everywhere with me since the very first one. But Apple only updates the Mini sporadically, and those updates sometimes feel like someone inside Apple Park picked its specs by closing their eyes and clicking randomly in an Excel sheet. The Mini is always a little underpowered, a little overpriced, and a little afield in Apple’s tablet lineup. We, the iPad Mini People, sometimes feel a little forgotten.
This year’s model , though, is an upgrade through and through. Apple made the screen larger and better, while making the iPad itself smaller and lighter. It upgraded the processor in a big way. It made the whole package more durable, so you can take it to more places and use it for more things. It actually feels like a tablet made for a reason, not just another occasional bone thrown to the small-tablet fans.
For the past week, I’ve been testing the midnight iPad Mini with cell service, 512GB of storage, and the nano-texture matte display coating. I really like it. It’s the best iPad Mini yet, and a huge leap over the previous model . The one in my hands also costs $1,249, and I cannot in good conscience tell you to buy it. Even the very cheapest version — Wi-Fi only, 128GB of storage, regular OLED display — starts at $699, by a wide margin the highest starting price ever for a Mini.
If you don’t already know the iPad Mini is your one true love, there’s probably a better iPad out there for you. But if you’re an iPad Mini Person and you can stomach the price? You’re getting the best Mini in years.
The Mini’s new display is its most important and most controversial upgrade. It now measures 8.5 inches instead of 8.3, and it’s now a 2316 x 1512 OLED panel instead of an LCD. The OLED gives the screen a little more dynamic range than the previous model, with brighter bright spots and darker dark spots. Its peak brightness is noticeably brighter than before, and its minimum brightness is low enough to be totally pleasant for reading in the dark (as long as you’re in dark mode). In general, it’s just a little more crisp and contrast-y, in a nice way; the old Mini’s display was the least of my worries, but the OLED is a solid improvement. The tablet I tested also has Apple’s nano-texture matte finish , which seems to dull and darken the screen slightly; on a particularly white background, the whole thing seems to shimmer. I suspect I’d like the OLED panel even more without it.
The nano-texture does, however, do an excellent job of reducing glare. The effect is actually really cool: The textured coating doesn’t extend to the bezels, so you can see a source of light or glare come in from the edge of the screen and then simply disappear as it hits the screen. So what you lose in pure screen fidelity, you gain in the ability to read on the iPad in a coffee shop without it reflecting the overhead lights like a mirror. The nano-texture option costs an extra $100, though, and requires you to upgrade to 256GB of storage, so you’re now looking at a $900 tablet. Spend the extra money on the cellular version or, better yet, don’t spend it at all.
For some reason, Apple has never deigned to put its ProMotion display tech on the iPad Mini, which has a refresh rate capped at 60Hz rather than the 120Hz you’ll get on most other recent Apple devices. This is such an odd spec choice that it has launched a bunch of conspiracy theories. Maybe it’s to make more people buy an iPhone Duo instead? Maybe it’s a 120Hz panel downgraded to 60Hz by software just to make people upgrade again next time? Apple’s answer, to Chris Lawley and others, has been something to the effect of “120Hz is irrelevant, OLED’s faster pixel response solves the problems.” I don’t agree. I don’t think the lack of ProMotion is an immediate and total dealbreaker, but refresh rates matter ! To games and high-touch creative apps, of course, but you notice the difference even with basic swiping and zooming. The Apple Pencil feels more juddery moving across my screen. On a 120Hz screen, I can scroll a browser page and still clearly read the text as it’s moving. With 60Hz, it gets blurry. In all these cases, even if you don’t explicitly see the difference, you really do feel it.
The most meaningful upgrade in the new Mini, at least for me and how I use my iPad, is that it is designed to be more or less waterproof and dustproof. Its IP67 rating means that the Mini got the highest possible score for protection from “solid foreign objects,” which for our purposes mostly just means dust won’t get inside, and is also “protected against the effects of temporary immersion in water.” It’s not quite as rugged as, say, the iPhone 18 Pro, and I don’t recommend using it as an underwater camera or anything, but your tablet should be fine as long as you don’t drop it in the tub and leave it for a while.
This increased ruggedness immediately changed my iPad usage in a couple of ways. I became less worried about handing the Mini to my toddler, whose general stickiness and penchant for spilling things no longer feel like threats. I also started using the Mini more in the kitchen — I love to cook with an iPad nearby for recipes and Community episodes, and it was nice not to be constantly guarding against flour explosions and water spills. At one point, the iPad Mini even came with me in the shower during a particularly close football game. It’s still kicking.
This is, for lack of a better word, the Field iPad.
The Mini’s IP rating is also the feature that finally made me see who Apple sees as the ideal iPad Mini user. This is, for lack of a better word, the Field iPad. We hear all the time about pilots who use Minis instead of sheaves of paperwork, but Apple also sees them in use on construction sites, oil rigs, doctor’s offices, and all kinds of other places. (It’s a fun rabbit hole, actually — can I interest you in an “explosion proof” last-gen Mini for $4,500 or so?) Apple’s goal with the Mini is not really to maximize performance, satisfy the pixel-peepers, or enhance creator workflows. It’s durability and usability. Body and screen.
Apple made a couple of changes to the Mini to receive its IP rating, like ditching the speaker holes and opting for what it calls an Acoustic Display. It means the sound fires out of the front panel rather than from speaker holes. (Some TVs currently work the same way.) It doesn’t sound any better than before, maybe a tiny bit bassier, but it also doesn’t sound worse, and if anything it’s slightly better to have the sound actually pointed at you instead of out the sides of the tablet. Mostly it’s a wash in service of the ruggedization, which is good enough for me.
The rest of the hardware is just wins all the way around. The A20 Pro chip, the chipset also on the iPhone 18 Pro (and the Duo ), benchmarks about 50 percent faster than the 2024 Mini for standard computing tasks, and about three times as fast for graphics-intensive ones. (The chip in my review unit has one more CPU core than the A20 Pro in the cheaper Minis; those will still be drastic improvements, but maybe a hair less so.) articles.title_orig: Saudi Aramco Profit Jumps Despite Damaging Attacks on Pipelines and Refineries
articles.title_zh: Saudi Aramco Profit Jumps Despite Damaging Attacks on Pipelines and Refineries
articles.content_orig:
Aramco reported a 9% rise in third-quarter adjusted net income on Tuesday on stronger refining margins.
The Saudi oil giant posted adjusted net income of $31.2 billion for the quarter, up from $28.6 billion a year earlier. The figure exceeded the median analyst consensus estimate of $30.66 billion, according to the company.
Aramco's downstream business, which processes crude oil into fuels and other products, posted adjusted earnings before interest and taxes of $10.3 billion, up 234% from a year earlier, driven by stronger refining margins.
"Geopolitical uncertainty and attacks on key energy facilities continued to amplify the global energy supply crisis in the third quarter of 2026, with serious implications for global energy security," Aramco CEO Amin H. Nasser said in a statement.
Nasser said the company's operational flexibility and supply network enabled it to continue delivering energy to customers despite the disruptions. Aramco is also exploring additional overseas storage capacity and alternative export routes to strengthen its global supply network.
The company generated $28.2 billion in free cash flow during the quarter, up from $23.6 billion a year earlier.
Aramco said its board declared a third-quarter base dividend of $21.9 billion, up 3.5% year on year, to be paid in the fourth quarter.
The company also said its major upstream projects remained on track and highlighted its acquisition of a 49% stake in Saudi artificial intelligence company HUMAIN.
– CNBC's Emma Graham contributed to this story.

articles.title_orig: Russia confirms new Ukraine peace talks as Melania Trump prepares to host ceasefire meeting
articles.title_zh: Russia confirms new Ukraine peace talks as Melania Trump prepares to host ceasefire meeting
articles.content_orig:
Russia on Tuesday confirmed that peace talks with Ukraine and the U.S. will go ahead next week in Abu Dhabi, while also signaling that a meeting between Presidents Vladimir Putin , Donald Trump and Xi Jinping to end the conflict was on the table.
Putin aide Vladimir ​Medinsky will serve ⁠as Moscow's chief negotiator ​at the talks in Abu Dhabi on Nov. 10-11, Kremlin spokesman ​Dmitry Peskov told reporters on a conference call, according to Reuters.
Separately, First Lady Melania Trump will bring Russian and Ukrainian representatives to the White House to discuss the local ceasefire in Kherson, the White House said Tuesday.
Monday saw the end of a six-day ceasefire in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky and surrounding areas in the Kherson region to allow for evacuation of residents, in a pause of hostilities that the White House said was brokered by the first lady.
Ukraine on Monday accused Russia of using the ceasefire to reinforce its military positions in the city.
The first lady's summit on Thursday will be "an extraordinary moment in American history," the White House said, but did not name the representatives who will attend. Melania Trump will deliver remarks on the Oleshky ceasefire at 11 a.m. ET Thursday, it added.
Peskov also said Tuesday the Kremlin hopes to finalize plans for a trilateral meeting between the leaders of Russia, the U.S., and China in the coming days. The comments follow earlier reports that these countries were planning to negotiate an end to the war in Ukraine, without Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy at the table.
Zelenskyy has said that any negotiations over Ukraine's future must include Kyiv.
"It can be acceptable only when we are at the table of negotiations," he said on Oct. 20, adding that he had discussed the proposal of a three-way meeting between the U.S., China, and Russia to negotiate an end to the nearly five-year full-scale war. "Nothing about Ukraine without Ukraine," he said.
Tensions between the U.S. and Ukraine have mounted over recent weeks amid continued strikes between Moscow and Kyiv, including on civilian and energy targets.
A series of moves by the Trump administration in October raised questions about Washington's reliability as Kyiv's most important military partner.
Tuesday's announcement follows U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff saying late Monday that Washington will mediate Ukraine-Russia peace talks in Abu Dhabi on Nov. 10-11, focusing on security arrangements, de-escalation and humanitarian issues.
Witkoff also said that U.S. negotiators will meet European and NATO officials in Brussels this week to discuss post-war security guarantees and Ukraine's reconstruction.

articles.title_orig: Europe on alert after supermarket freezers hit by cyber-attacks in nine countries
articles.title_zh: Europe on alert after supermarket freezers hit by cyber-attacks in nine countries
articles.content_orig:
A spate of cyber-attacks that hit supermarket chains across at least 10 European countries on Monday has prompted European Union officials to warn of a deliberate attempt to disrupt the food supply chain.
Supermarkets have reported problems in Belgium, Estonia, Finland, Ireland, Italy, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Portugal, Germany and Sweden, and the significant increase in freezer temperatures has forced retailers to discard food.
Temperatures in chains across Europe reportedly rose as high as 50C (122F).
No-one has yet admitted carrying out the cyber-attacks.
The European Union has raised concerns about the attacks, which come three weeks after a cyber-attack disrupted as many as 700 French grocery stores, causing food losses estimated at tens of millions of euros.
The security of refrigeration systems as well as other devices that can be monitored remotely has heightened concerns about government-backed hybrid attacks.
The EU's food and agriculture commissioner, Christophe Hansen, said the bloc was taking the incidents very seriously and warned of further disruption in the future.
Commission spokesman Thomas Regnier was careful not to attribute blame, but said: "These incidents of course show once again how cyber-attacks can disrupt essential services and affect citizens' daily lives."
"These are not isolated incidents and of course we have to be collectively resilient and prepared for such cyber incidents."
In Italy , Giorgia Meloni's government called a meeting with intelligence chiefs, but said the impact was "currently very limited" and most of the food distribution chain had up-to-date security systems able to fend off such attacks.
At least four Co-op supermarkets in Sicily and one business in Tuscany were affected, according to the national cybersecurity agency.
Meloni's office said those businesses affected were "mostly still equipped with obsolete security systems, with interfaces directly exposed to the internet and inadequate authentication mechanisms".
Belgian supermarkets were among those hardest-hit, with dozens of stores reporting refrigeration failures. Federal prosecutors have opened an investigation.
Mathieu Tilman, a manager at a Delhaize supermarket in Belgium, said he was shocked by this kind of attack: "I don't even understand how anyone could do this... How can we end up throwing away so much food? I find it truly distressing. In moments like these, you just feel like quitting your job."
In Ireland , 13 SuperValu stores were impacted by what the chain's owner, Musgrave Group, called a cyber-incident. "Replenishment of chilled and frozen ranges in the affected stores is well under way," a spokesman said on Monday.
A small number of corner shops in the Netherlands also suffered disruption. Last month, supermarket chain Albert Heijn had to take several services offline because of a separate cyber-attack.
There was disruption to refrigeration systems at the Rewe Büsken supermarket in western Germany after a cyber-attack on system provider Danfoss, the company told the BBC. Its systems have been back in operation since Monday afternoon.
In Portugal , the Mosqueteiros group said that incidents at seven Intermarché stores had been linked to a cyberattack, which "appears to have targeted an external service provider responsible for managing the refrigeration systems".
Swedish chain ICA also said "a limited number" of its stores had experienced refrigeration problems, without confirming a cyber-attack, and Sweden's national cyber-security agencies said they were monitoring the incident.
In Finland , irregular temperatures were detected in a few smaller grocery stores belonging to the Kesko group, which said it was investigating the issue.
In Estonia , at least one supermarket was attacked by hackers who raised the temperature in the refrigeration units to 50C, public broadcaster ERR reported.
In the UK , the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) has warned British retailers to update the software on fridge temperature controls.
The agency said the country was likely to suffer an AI-powered cyber-attack on critical national infrastructure within two years.
Richard Horne, the head of the National Cyber Security Centre, told BBC Radio 4's Today programme there were a couple of instances in the UK where "vulnerable technology has been exploited" after the cyber-attacks.
"We don't know the full impact, but we do know there are a couple of instances where vulnerable technology has been exploited and we're working with those organisations."
Asked if there was any evidence that supermarkets in Britain or freezers of the same make or model had been targeted, Horne said: "It's not just supermarkets, it's through the whole food supply chain, and we've been working through the night alerting organisations where we can see they've got exposed technology that's vulnerable in this way."

articles.title_orig: Santoli: AI bull market almost surely needs tech stocks to recover to keep advancing
articles.title_zh: Santoli: AI bull market almost surely needs tech stocks to recover to keep advancing
articles.content_orig:
Get Mike Santoli's Market Memo in your inbox first. SUBSCRIBE HERE
The road to bull-market glory does not run through Walmart and Berkshire Hathaway and Eli Lilly.
There's been a virtual buying panic in traditionally defensive, high-quality stocks over the past few weeks, a near-equal-and-opposite offset to the selling pressure in semiconductors and AI-build-out spenders. The three stocks above — the only members of the $1 trillion market-cap club not in Big Tech – have collectively added $550 billion in market value in the past month, almost making up for what Alphabet has lost.
The Nasdaq-100 and the S&P 500 Low Volatility ETF (SPLV) are rushing toward one another in a satisfying picture of symmetry that nonetheless reflects an almost comical level of tactical rotation executed by an investment community accustomed to playing one factor against another.
While this to-and-fro has so far protected the S&P 500 as a whole from an appreciable setback for months, it has left it stymied around levels that date back to May — before we got two earnings-reporting seasons showing 30% annual profit growth.
A week ago here , I suggested the AI theme was nearing a make-or-break moment to stage a recovery or risk surrendering its leadership status and destabilizing the broader market. Thus far, this trade has failed to respond to moderate oversold conditions or a run of cosmetically strong hyperscaler quarterly results, further loosening its grip on the benefit of the doubt.
In stressed markets undergoing soul-searching about the long-term bullish thesis, prices often need to travel further to find buyers with conviction while the market action must disappoint dip-buyers to extinguish complacency. Hard to know if we're there, but presumably we're now closer.
The Nasdaq-100 closed Monday right at its 200-day moving average, off almost 11% from its record high. After an enervating failed Monday-morning bounce attempt, the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index finished down another 3.8% and settled under the late-July low that was set as the Situational Awareness hedge fund was finished liquidating.
"Markets did not get the memo that bearish seasonal pressure typically subsides in mid-October and instead ended the month with some of the most acute selling pressure that has been realized during the late-summer/early-fall period," notes JPMorgan technical strategist Jason Hunter. He's advising clients to remain on the defensive "until we see clear evidence of a bottoming process on the charts or until there are clear signs of capitulation."
This is a time-tested playbook, though many a sharp market pullback has ended without what would qualify as unqualified capitulation.
The market action is winning some plaudits for the way non-tech stocks have held up better, many groups benefiting from the "quality" rotation while abandoned consumer cyclicals get a reprieve from easing oil prices and the slide in the 10-year Treasury yield back below 5%.
This gives active managers plenty to do in playing against a highly concentrated and tech-dependent S&P 500. But I'll continue to argue that the bull market built on the AI story will almost surely need the AI story to get back on track to keep advancing. A prolonged period when the equal-weight S&P 500 outperforms the market-cap-weighted version is otherwise known – usually – as a bear market.
The AI-related stocks' weighting in the S&P 500 is off the highs but remains near 45%, according to Morgan Stanley.
As the chart shows, AI has wobbled relative to the rest of the market during this uptrend before reasserting itself.  But there's a trickier element to the current gut check: In prior phases of the buildout, the key limiting bottleneck gave investors something to buy in order to exploit it.
The initial scarcity of GPUs meant to own Nvidia above all else from 2023 through 2024. When cloud capacity, power and cooling were found to be the crucial scarce resources, hyperscaler stocks worked and the AI-adjacent industrials were drastically revalued. Then memory emerged as the chokepoint and Micron and Sandisk went stratospheric.
Now, as Nvidia's Jensen Huang has said, capital is the constraint and that not only leaves no asset to buy, but it raises the cost of capital broadly as the mega-caps go free-cash-flow-negative.
Overlapping feedback loops and scrambled correlations across the markets and the real economy have further sapped investor conviction. Treasury yields no longer move with oil but largely with AI-capex sentiment, with both in retreat lately. AI-stock setbacks also mute inflation momentum and the equity wealth effect, meaning fewer Federal Reserve rate hikes are anticipated now versus a month ago.
This all probably sounds like an elaborate trap, and it has become one for the previously crowded trades. Could this reflect the end game for the AI-exuberance market chapter, which as I keep pointing out peaked around the SpaceX IPO in June? Impossible to say for sure, but if it were, I'm not sure things would look much different to this point.
But I don't want to dismiss the possibility that a lot of the known challenges are largely reflected in prices.
I argued in August that we should assume the valuation peak for this cycle was in. We've now retrenched to a forward P/E of 18.5 on the S&P 500 from 23 a year ago and the Nasdaq-100 at 20x is at the slimmest premium to the S&P 500 valuation in nine years. I'm on board with the idea that the market is telling us companies are now "over-earning," but if nothing else there is less valuation risk now than in recent months.
Sentiment toward AI stocks is in the dumps. Funds' positioning in tech has retreated below neutral. Important trading lows this year have happened near the turn of the month on March 30 and July 29, and the Nasdaq-100's relative-strength reading is exactly as oversold as it was at those turns.
So, stay alert for possible relief bounces that could evolve into something more consequential if indeed the midterm elections pass in a way that allows traders to unclench a bit into the year's home stretch.
John Kolovos of Macro Risk Advisors on the latest reading: "Similar to valuation, sentiment is not a timing tool, but it is getting harder and harder to find any bulls, as a near-perfect storm of tight financial conditions is being met with tech earnings that have gone from bad to worse in the blink of an eye."
-Another good big-picture conversation on the practical business and investment implications of the next phase of AI proliferation on Patrick O'Shaughnessy's Invest Like the Best podcast , this one with investor Cliff Sosin. His comparison of AI infrastructure economics to internet connectivity providers and his argument for how most of the productivity boost will go toward "consumer surplus" rather than corporate profits are particularly interesting.
-For my birthday Monday, my colleague and friend Sara Eisen wondered how I would write a birthday message to myself. I immediately regretted suggesting she ask ChatGPT, which generated this credible and somewhat embarrassing result :
"Another year older, though the longer-term trend remains constructive. Some modest deterioration in the underlying internals, perhaps, but nothing that suggests a decisive breakdown.
"The candles on the cake are approaching historically elevated levels, though valuation concerns have persisted for years without derailing the advance. At this stage, the key question isn't whether I've gotten older — that's largely priced in — but whether the wisdom gains can continue to offset the inevitable compression in energy multiples.
"For now, I'm maintaining a cautiously optimistic outlook, with upside optionality, downside support from family and friends, and no immediate need for Fed intervention. Happy birthday to me. The secular bull market remains intact."

articles.content_orig:

Two Ryanair flights have been searched following anonymous tips regarding potential bomb threats, hours after several planes were forced into an emergency landing.
Sources told the BBC that the Ryanair flights - one originating from Lisbon and one from Dublin - had been forced into an emergency landing.
It came hours after a bomb scare forced a passenger plane from London to make an emergency landing in Poland on Tuesday, while three other threats grounded flights from Manchester, Copenhagen and Israel.
The Polish airline LOT flight from Heathrow was carrying 181 people when an alert brought it down at Warsaw-Modlin airport. Security services were still verifying the threat and the international airport affected was temporarily closed.
The Boeing 737 MAX had been due to land at Warsaw Chopin airport when the warning came in at 8.54am GMT. Bomb disposal experts reportedly checked the flight and passengers’ luggage after it touched down at Modlin seven minutes later.
The Independent approached Ryanair and London Heathrow for comment .
Follow our live updates below...
At least seven flights across Europe were grounded on Tuesday following bomb scares.
A Ryanair flight from Lisbon was searched following an anonymous tip about a potential bomb threat, the airline said.
Another Ryanair flight from Dublin was also searched, they added.
A flight from London Heathrow to Poland had to divert to another Warsaw airport due to an alert.
And another flight from Copenhagen to Poland received a bomb scare but landed as planned in Warsaw.
A flight from Manchester to Murcia in Spain received a threat, but that later turned out to be a hoax.
A flight from Israel landed in Bulgaria’s Sofia following a bomb threat.
Bulgaria’s transport ministry also reported a Bergamo flight operated by Wizz Air had to land in Sofia.
And a Dublin flight operated by Ryanair also had to land in Sofia, they said. It was unclear whether the Dublin flight was the same one as reported earlier by Ryanair.
A flight from Luton to Sofia was also forced to make an emergency landing in Budapest following a suspected bomb threat.
Bomb threats were made against two planes traveling from Bergamo and Dublin to Bulgaria's capital Sofia, Bulgaria’s transport ministry said in a statement to Reuters on Tuesday.
Both landed safely and no explosive devices were found on inspection.
The Bergamo flight was operated by Wizz Air and was carrying 176 passengers, the statement said. The Dublin flight, operated by Ryanair, had 185 passengers on board.
Adam Szabłowski, spokesperson for Warsaw Modlin Airport, told tvn24.pl: “A plane from London landed at Modlin Airport at 10.01am with 181 people on board.
“The airport has been closed. We are waiting for bomb disposal experts.”
The airport said in a statement that the plane was directed to a designated area after landing and would remain there until the authorities, including bomb disposal teams, can advise.
Passengers were told to wait in the arrival lounge while checks were being carried out. Modlin later announced on Tuesday that the rest of the airport had resumed operations.
Warsaw-Chopin remained open on Tuesday, a spokesperson for the airport said.
Warsaw has two airports: Chopin is within the city limits and Modlin, mostly used by budget airlines, is about 22 miles from the capital.
While no one has claimed responsibility for the scares, the incidents reflect growing concerns in Europe about hybrid threats to infrastructure amid growing security tensions since Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine.
An explosive-laden drone was found near a Ukrainian plane at the Leipzig/Halle airport in east Germany in August, prompting a counterterrorism investigation.
Germany accused Russia of responsibility for the attack.Moscow has repeatedly denied involvement in sabotage or hybrid warfare operations and has not commented on Tuesday’s incidents in Poland.
The incidents come a day after a WizzAir flgiht from London Luton to Bulgaria’s Sofia was diverted to Budapest following a reported mid-air bomb threat. The scare was ultimately shown to be a false alarm.
A bomb scare forced a passenger plane from London to make an emergency landing in Poland on Tuesday, while three other threats grounded flights from Manchester, Copenhagen and Israel.
- A Polish airline LOT Boeing 737 from Heathrow was carrying 181 people when an alert brought it down on Tuesday morning at Warsaw-Modlin airport, diverted from Warsaw Chopin.
- A second bomb threat was reported on a Scandinavian SAS flight from Copenhagen to Warsaw, which was forced to land at Chopin Airport and was also being checked.
- A third threat was reported on a Ryanair flight carrying 114 passengers from Manchester that landed in Murcia in southern Spain, according to Diari ARA.
- Separately, a plane flying from Israel landed at Sofia airport after a bomb threat was received by email, local media reported on Tuesday. Counter-terrorism units were checking the plane for possible explosive devices.
It was not immediately clear whether the threats were linked.
A spokesperson for the UK’s civil aviation authority (CAA) tells The Independent that they are aware of the reports of bomb threats on flights departing from the UK.
They say they are unable to comment on the specific incidents.

articles.title_orig: Apple CEO John Ternus criticized for ‘scripted’ approach to first earnings call
articles.title_zh: Apple CEO John Ternus criticized for ‘scripted’ approach to first earnings call
articles.content_orig:
Investors didn’t seem overly happy about yesterday’s Apple earnings call despite the record results . That likely reflects the company’s cautious take on margins in the current quarter, but some have also criticized what they describe as a very “scripted” approach by new CEO John Ternus .
Bloomberg was the biggest critic, describing it as a “timid” performance that left analysts “sorely disappointed” …
Bloomberg’s Dave Lee didn’t hold back.
Apple investors and fans hoping to get an insight into the philosophy of new Chief Executive Officer John Ternus on Monday were left sorely disappointed. The 51-year-old’s first earnings call was a timid affair, with Ternus taking cover behind a carefully written script as analysts peppered him with questions.
Newly minted CEO plays it safe during his first high-stakes earnings call? Absolutely shocking! Seriously, what did Bloomberg expect?
Lee acknowledged that the slump in pre-market trading will have been largely driven by Apple’s caution about rising expenses in the current quarter. The company said that memory costs were continuing to rise and that building out Siri AI data centers we’re going to add to the RAM bill. But he argued that Ternus missed an opportunity to talk up the company.
In front of Ternus on Monday night was a chance to counteract the gloom and doom by instilling in Wall Street the fundamentals of the Ternus Doctrine — what he sees Apple becoming under his tenure, the “product guy” taking the company to a new era of innovation. Instead, he spoke like a man glancing at the clock and wishing the minutes away.
Fortune’s Sebastian Herrera was less vocal but echoed some of the criticism.
Ternus fielded some questions but also delegated answers to Chief Financial Officer Kevan Parekh and Chief Operating Officer Sabih Khan, who Apple said would participate in earnings calls moving forward, something the company hasn’t done for years. Ternus projected confidence on the call, but he appeared to stick mostly to scripted marketing points.
It will of course take Ternus some time to develop his own style when it comes to all of the varied aspects of the role, including addressing analysts in earnings calls, but I thought he took a measured but optimistic approach. Given the famously reticent style of his predecessor, the criticism strikes me as rather odd.
What’s your take? Please share in the comments.

articles.title_orig: King to open Commonwealth summit as Burnham begins talks on slavery apology
articles.title_zh: King to open Commonwealth summit as Burnham begins talks on slavery apology
articles.content_orig:
King Charles III is opening the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (Chogm) in Antigua and Barbuda - you can watch live above
In his speech to leaders, he addresses the slave trade and says the "shameful chapter of history is one that fills my heart with horror"
These are some of the most powerful words the King has ever said on the slave trade and he addressed the issue early in the speech , our senior royal correspondent writes
Also at the summit is British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who says he is "open" to a formal apology from the UK over slavery, but said reparations were "not the right answer"
As part of talks with fellow leaders, Burnham is expected to set out plans for a "debt reset" to support Commonwealth countries dealing with the growing cost of paying interest
The Commonwealth leaders' summit is held every two years and allows leaders and representatives of the 56 nations to discuss the future of the partnership
Edited by Matt Spivey, with senior royal correspondent Daniela Relph and political editor Chris Mason in Antigua
Concluding his speech, the King says he has only had time in this speech to mention "some of the ways" in which the Commonwealth is able to use its "unique advantage" to deliver tangible change.
Addressing the gathered leaders, he says the leadership of the Commonwealth is "in your hands".
"Each of you has the opportunity to make the greatest possible difference, I pray that over the coming days you will embrace this opportunity and commit yourselves to action," he says.
Above all, he says he trusts that each of the gathered leaders will commit to a Commonwealth in which "our young people can look to the future with greater confidence and purpose".
He ends by saying that he hopes people can draw inspiration from "this remarkable family of nations" as he himself has "always done".
The King mentions "brutal conflicts" the world is facing, and calls climate change a "catastrophic reality", which is leaving nature under constant attack.
He also says technology is transforming societies and economies "at dizzying speed", with little certainty about where it will lead us.
Together, these challenges "comprise the crisis of our time," the King continues.
The King then says that while the Commonwealth can't provide all of the solutions required, it does provide the opportunity to work together.
The monarch says the theme of this Chogm, accelerating partnerships and investment for a prosperous Commonwealth, represents a "vital opportunity" for us all.
On climate change, he adds that large ocean states have contributed little to the effects of climate change but are among those carrying the "greatest cost".
He says he is looking forward to hearing how Commonwealth leaders work with others such as the private sector on innovative proposals to tackle climate change.
Daniela Relph Senior royal correspondent
These are some of the most powerful words the King has ever said on the slave trade.
He addressed the UK role in the slave trade early on in the speech and spoke personally of his own horror and profound personal sorrow.
The King continues, saying that the more he has furthered his "understanding of the issues" the more committed he has become to "address the wrongs of the past with action for the future".
This includes, he says, improving access to education, investing in jobs and opportunities, encouraging "inter-Commonwealth trade" and tackling climate change.
"I have always felt there is so much that can be done to help lift up those who struggle against hardship," he says, adding that he has "always tried to play my part in doing just that".
He says the Commonwealth today is not just a product of the past, but a "response of the world of today", adding that "its vocation is more compelling than ever... in a desperately troubled world".
The King continues by saying the prism of time can be "both clarifying and distorting", but its consequences "resonate with contemporary force".
He says: "Our history inspires us, can appal us yet it can always teach us."
The monarch says the transatlantic trade in enslaved persons "still cast a shadow" over the Caribbean islands and other members of the Commonwealth.
"As I've said before, that shameful chapter of history is one that fills my heart with horror and my soul with the most profound personal sorrow," the Kings says.
He adds that character and courage can combine to overcome the "most monstrous injustice" as it did with the determination to end the international slave trade.
King Charles then pays tribute to the diversity of the Commonwealth, which he says has "mattered greatly" to him throughout his life.
None of us would be here today if not for our history, he continues, and says this history "is not ours to choose or change".
Our inheritance includes both our forebears' achievements and failures, he adds.
King Charles begins by saying he and the Queen are "delighted" to attend the 28th Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (Chogm), and adds it is "sobering" to think that he attended the first one 30 years ago.
He thanks the government of Antigua and Barbuda for their "remarkable hospitality".
"For one of the smallest nations on earth, your impact in the world is tremendous, and I think there is great truth is the saying 'small island, big vibes'," he says.
King Charles on stage at the Commonwealth summit in Antigua.
King Charles III is now standing on stage to deliver his speech at the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (Chogm) in Antigua.
We will be bringing you updates here and you can watch the speech live at the top of this page.
Commonwealth Secretary-General Shirley Botchwey describes the Commonwealth as an "indispensable agent of change" in a "world of rupture and uncertainty".
"Citizens from St John's to Sydney, Manchester to Mombasa are living through profound uncertainty," she says.
She says the goal of the summit is to "build a new model of partnership" capable of responding to the "scale of challenges we face".
She adds that too many Commonwealth nations are "held back by the rules on debt treatments" and says Commonwealth nations are working together to "change the international financial system".
The prime minister of host nation Antigua and Barbuda is first to speak on stage at the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (Chogm).
Gaston Browne says hosting the meeting is "more than a privilege" and tells the King: "We are deeply honoured by your presence as Head of the Commonwealth, together with her Majesty the Queen."
He adds at the last Chogm, in Samoa in 2024, nations agreed the time had come for a "truthful respectful conversation on reparatory justice".
"We must now carry that commitment forward through structured inclusive dialogue on the enduring consequences of slavery and colonialism," he says.
Chris Mason Political editor, in Antigua
Fifty-six Commonwealth countries are represented here.
This once-every-two-year gathering has a habit of playing out noisily, as this club with a long and often awkward history now thrashes around for purpose and a future.
British diplomats see a value in a collection of countries, including many small ones, scattered around the world with a combined population of 2.7 billion - and not involving America, China or Russia.
But after the summit in Samoa two years ago was dominated by reparations, this time the UK has sought to attempt to neutralise or at least cool the issue in advance.
A formal apology is in the offing in the next year and there's talk of trying to ease the burden of spiralling debt interest payments.
Daniela Relph Senior royal correspondent, in Antigua
Queen Elizabeth II was always a strong supporter of the Commonwealth. The King has picked up that baton - seeing it as a force for good.

This new PS5 version brings significant improvements over the original PS4 bundle of the two intense shooters, so they are worth revisiting again if you haven't already. Here's what to expect on PS5:

articles.title_orig: Yum Brands earnings beat estimates, but cyclospora outbreak weighs on Taco Bell
articles.title_zh: Yum Brands earnings beat estimates, but cyclospora outbreak weighs on Taco Bell
articles.content_orig:
Yum Brands on Tuesday reported earnings that beat expectations, but a cyclospora outbreak linked to iceberg lettuce at Taco Bell weighed on the company's same-store sales growth.
However, Yum said Taco Bell, which the company considers a "growth engine" for its business, has since rebounded.
"Since the end of September, Taco Bell U.S. has been outpacing the [quick-service restaurant] industry on same-store sales growth," Yum CEO Chris Turner said in a statement.
Taco Bell's same-store sales are up about 1% so far in the fourth quarter, CFO Ranjith Roy said on the company's earnings conference call Tuesday. In the last four weeks ended Friday, same-store sales have risen 3% compared with the year-ago period.
Here's what the company reported compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:
Yum reported fiscal third-quarter net income of $1.62 billion, or $5.92 per share, up from $397 million, or $1.41 per share, a year earlier.
Excluding gains from its divestiture of Pizza Hut and other items, the restaurant company earned $1.56 per share.
Net sales rose 4% to $2.05 billion.
During the quarter, Yum completed its divestiture of Pizza Hut. It closed the sale of the pizza chain's business in mainland China to Yum China on Aug. 7 and sold the rest of Pizza Hut to LongRange Capital on Sept. 1. The company's third-quarter results include Pizza Hut up until those dates.
Excluding Pizza Hut, Yum's same-store sales were flat for the quarter as Taco Bell weighed on the company's overall results. Taco Bell's same-store sales declined by 4% as diners temporarily pulled back on visits due to the foodborne illness outbreak .
Yum executives previously said the weekend of July 18 saw the most severe impact to sales, but trends have improved since then.
Taco Bell's most loyal customers returned faster, Yum said, thanks in part to weekly Tuesday deals for loyalty program members after the cyclospora outbreak took over headlines.
Traffic from "medium" and "light" customers has bounced back to about 95% of prior levels, while visits from "heavy" users is back to normal, Roy said. To attract more casual diners, Taco Bell has been relying on star power, like a collaboration with pop star Olivia Rodrigo on a pink-colored Mountain Dew Baja Blast.
Outside of the U.S., Taco Bell's much smaller international business reported same-store sales growth of 5%.
KFC's same-store sales ticked up 1%, helped by system sales growth in China and Europe. The U.S., now the chicken chain's third-largest market, saw system sales shrink 6% in the quarter.
Like Restaurant Brands International's Popeyes , KFC has struggled in the U.S. amid a wave of new competitors and more budget-conscious consumers. Its home market represents only about 5% of KFC's operating profit, but it remains a symbolically important part of the business for Yum investors.
During the quarter, KFC U.S. launched popcorn chicken, which sold out in many restaurants. However, Yum said the limited-time menu item was not enough to offset the successful Hot & Spicy Wings and Potato Wedges promotion during the year-ago period.
Globally, KFC is trying to become "the most modern chicken QSR ," Turner said on the company's earnings conference call. To achieve that lofty goal, he said the chain will roll out buzzy promotions, a new brand identity, and a wider menu that includes upgraded sauces and more beverages.

articles.title_orig: Indian tourist killed after two helicopters collide near Everest base camp
articles.title_zh: Indian tourist killed after two helicopters collide near Everest base camp
articles.content_orig:
An Indian tourist has died after two helicopters collided while attempting to land near the base camp of Mount Everest, two officials have confirmed to the BBC.
Verified footage of the crash showed the helicopter blades of the two aircraft clipping each other as they came into land at around 08:15 local time (02:30 GMT) in Pheriche, approximately 12km (7 miles) south of Mount Everest Base Camp.
Helicopter company Fishtail Air named the man  killed in the crash as Vasanth Kumar Balaramudu.
The helicopter company said one of its vehicles was involved in the collision and that another passenger and the helicopter's captain had been injured.
The injured passengers and crew members on board were rescued and taken to Kathmandu, Fishtail Air added in a statement.
The injured passenger was a tourist from New Zealand, an official of Solukhumbu district, Bhupendra Thapa, told BBC Nepal.
The other helicopter involved was operated by Air Dynasty and had been carrying cargo, the company said.
It was operated by one crew member who sustained no injuries, it added.
A spokesman for Nepal's Civil Aviation Authority, Gyanendra Bhul, said: "It appears the accident happened when two helicopters... attempted to land at the same spot."
In the video footage of the incident, the weather conditions look clear and no strong wind effects are visible. One helicopter appears to be making a more rapid descent than the other.
Helicopters are widely used for transport in the Himalayan nation due to its challenging terrain. But its rapidly changing weather conditions and high altitude often make aviation operations hazardous.
The village of Pheriche, located on the trekking route to the summit of the world's tallest mountain, Mount Everest, is just over 4,000m (13,120ft) above sea level.
Climbing expeditions to Everest and Ama Dablam mountain are currently under way in the region, as autumn is a popular climbing season.

articles.title_orig: Charity warns about damage of over-foraging fungi
articles.title_zh: Charity warns about damage of over-foraging fungi
articles.content_orig:
The impacts of over-foraging natural spaces, particularly in protected areas, can damage habitats, a Devon charity has said.
The Woodland Trust said unsustainable harvesting of plants - and particularly fungi - could put wildlife under pressure.
Joe Middleton, site manager for the Woodland Trust, said he had seen commercial mushroom pickers "wiping out everything on the path edges they can find".
Under Section 4 of the Theft Act 1968, it is "perfectly legal to forage for fruit, foliage, flowers, and fungi on any land, provided they are wild and collected strictly for personal use", but "foraging becomes criminal theft if you pick wild plants for commercial sale or reward without permission".
Middleton said: "I have seen commercial pickers, dropped off in mini buses with bags for life, laden heavy with mushrooms and they are going through and they are wiping out everything on the path edges they can find, trampling the forest floor."
The majority of mushrooms are not edible to humans, so picking them can be potentially dangerous.
In the autumn they are an essential source of food for animals such as deer and badgers, all the way down to things that live in the soil such as worms and woodlice.
Middleton said: "If we start decimating the population, it takes their food source away.
"They can't just get up and move, a lot of our wildlife is dependent on this fungi. We just need to be a bit more sustainable in what we are doing."
Entering private property without a landowner's consent to forage is a civil rather than criminal offence. However, foraging is heavily restricted or illegal in local Sites of Special Scientific Interest (SSSIs) or protected areas like Woodland Trust sites.
Using ingredients from local areas is very fashionable on social media at the moment.
John Dobson, from the Refectory restaurant near Ugborough, said he thought there were other factors too.
He said: "The rising cost of ingredients; they're getting really, really expensive, so I think that could be encouraging people to go out and source things from other places. There is also a lack of education about the impact."
Dobson added he made sure to forage responsibly, only taking a third of what he found, and doing so with any landowner's permission.
Middleton said foraging was a great way to connect with nature, but he wanted to encourage people to enjoy woodlands without taking any of it home with them too.
He said: "We've gone a long way from Victorian times in terms of taking everything we see and pinning it and netting it.
"Now we are in a technological age. We can just use our phones, take great pictures; we can look without touching - particularly in a protected place."
Penzance-based forager, wild food guide and founder of Wild Walks South West  Rachel Lambert said: "It's always an issue.
"It's one of the fundamental rules, guidelines of foraging, is to consider who else is foraging in the area, and that includes all the other non-human beings - the wildlife in the area."
She said people should only take what they needed and only select things which were abundant.
She added foraging "takes time" and people should think about their impact on nature.

articles.title_orig: Midterm elections could jolt stocks if Democrats sweep Congress
articles.title_zh: Midterm elections could jolt stocks if Democrats sweep Congress
articles.content_orig:
The stock market is not yet pricing in a Democratic sweep of Congress — despite some polls and most prediction markets pointing that way — so that scenario could weigh on share prices Wednesday, according to investors and analysts.
Republicans managing to keep control could cause a short-term relief rally, they said.
Short-term moves aside, the typical post-midterm pattern in the months ahead is bullish. But some wonder if the market could buck the positive historical trend this time because the S&P 500 is already up so much this year going into the election.
As far as certain stocks to watch, a big Democratic win on Tuesday night — especially in the Texas governor race — could add fuel to an AI stock sell-off on the notion that more data center restrictions would gain momentum nationally. Defense stocks could come under pressure on fears of limits on spending.
Polls are pointing to a Democratic victory in the House and a toss-up in the Senate. Prediction markets have been more favorable to Democrats, calling for a blue sweep .
While investors are signaling "begrudging acceptance" to a base case scenario that there will indeed be a Democratic sweep, that's not how they're positioning, said Tobin Marcus, head of U.S. policy and politics at Wolfe Research. The firm's recent survey data among more than 100 institutional investors suggests they are not strongly positioned for any particular result.
"Investors seem to have a significant dose of skepticism about whether the final outcome is going to be quite as favorable to Democrats as the polling suggests," Marcus told CNBC, noting that the firm shares the view that the "polling is likely overstating Democratic strength."
JPMorgan sees a blue wave knocking the S&P 500 by about a half percent on Wednesday.
On the other hand, if Republicans end up retaining both chambers of Congress, that could spur a rally, said Sameer Samana, head of global equities and real assets at Wells Fargo Investment Institute.
"From a certainty standpoint, the market knows what to do with Republicans holding both chambers," he said.
Citigroup strategists said Monday that Republicans losing the House but managing to keep the Senate could be "a tailwind for equities into year-end." JPMorgan traders predict up to a 1% pop on Wednesday if Republicans hold on to that chamber.
Looking past any short-term move, stocks tend to rally after the midterms have concluded. In fact, the S&P 500 was up one year out after all midterm elections going back to the early 1980s.
But the S&P 500 has already recorded double-digit gains so far in 2026, so some on Wall Street worry that investors are being overly complacent heading into this year's elections.
During midterm election years, the S&P 500 has typically averaged a 14% drawdown at some point in the second half of the year found Jonathan Krinsky, chief market technician at BTIG.
"The reason stocks often perform well in November during midterms is because [the S&P 500] typically is weak INTO the elections. We have the opposite setup this year," Krinsky wrote last week. "Therefore, while consensus is that we see a post midterm rally, we think the opposite is actually more likely."
It's not helping that the broader market has recently come under significant pressure due to turbulence in the AI trade, which led the Nasdaq Composite to post its worst day since June on Friday. AI shares led the market lower again on Monday.
A strong showing from Democrats in Tuesday's midterm elections could pressure the trade even more .
At the state level, increased Democratic control is probably a headwind for stocks associated with data centers and technological capital equipment, analysts said.
"It [would solidify] the early kind of cautionary signs in different states around the advancement of AI infrastructure," Rob Rains at Washington Analysis told CNBC.
Goldman Sachs strategists said this week that a Democratic Congress "might limit data center tax incentives, but a national moratorium looks unlikely in any election outcome."
One example would be Texas — a key hub of the data-center buildout. A surprise loss there by Republican Gov. Greg Abbott has the "potential to spook" the market in the short term, Wolfe's Marcus said.
A blue wave might pressure defense shares, while boosting health care stocks, analysts and investors said.
"A substantial Democratic sweep could limit real spending growth unless a broader agreement increases both defense and health-care funding," said Alex Sagal, global equity analyst at Wells Fargo Investment Institute. However, he noted that the earnings outlook for the defense industry looks "stable to modestly positive."
Wolfe Research's Marcus said that healthcare is going to be "the biggest focus," as Democrats will push for restoring expired Affordable Care Act enhanced premium subsidies or unwinding some of the Medicaid reforms in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act .
"Healthcare stocks have been doing really well lately," Jed Ellerbroek, portfolio manager at Argent Capital Management, said to CNBC. "I think part of that is the anti-AI trade, but I also think part of it is just optimism that Democrats are taking over."
Ellerbroek is keeping his eye on hospital-related stocks such as HCA Healthcare and Tenet Healthcare as well as health insurers like UnitedHealth and Centene .
Financials was the worst S&P 500 sector in early 2026 on the heels of President Donald Trump calling on Congress to pass a law that would cap credit card interest rates at 10% . While the sector has been able to notch gains since, with its year-to-date rise now at around 3%, things could get more unstable for the group under Democratic control.
"Democrats will come in wanting to show tangible progress on the affordability issue, and that means targeting sectors that are front and center in consumer budgets," said Evercore ISI's Matthew Aks. "We know Trump has populist instincts, populist leanings, and could he pick a couple of issues and decide to team up with the Democrats on those issues and target those industries in a populist way? Absolutely."
Given that Democratic control is often associated with increased regulation, while Republican control is thought to promote deregulation, Democrats could be interested in passing credit card rate caps if they come out victorious.
"I think if Democrats have control of one or both chambers, they would try to pass it and see if they could get Trump to either sign it or force him to veto it, and that would let Democrats kind of score a political point," Aks said.
Trump could restart the war against Iran after holding off any major strikes leading up to the midterms, a move that could upend the overall market and cause energy stocks to outperform. Crude oil prices jumped more than 10% in October, though they gave a lot of that gain back on Monday.
Gasoline prices stood at $4.17 a gallon on average nationwide Sunday, a nearly 40% increase compared to the same period last year, per AAA.
"If there are escalations, that could obviously put upward pressure on prices just ahead of Thanksgiving," said Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysts at Gas Buddy, "which is also when Americans have really staunch traditions in terms of driving to friends and family."
If Trump decides to take forceful action, it could snuff out hope for a typical post-midterm year-end rally.
Evercore ISI said the S&P 500 could retreat by double-digits to end the year at 6,800 as oil spikes if the president "moves to kinetic escalation in Iran ahead of seating the new Congress in January" and Democrats take Congress.
— With reporting by Sarah Min, Tobias Burns and Spencer Kimball
