articles.title_orig: Palantir Stock Tumbles Even as Earnings Get Big Boost From U.S. Customers
articles.title_zh: Palantir Stock Tumbles Even as Earnings Get Big Boost From U.S. Customers
articles.content_orig:
Palantir beat Wall Street's third-quarter estimates after the bell on Monday, with U.S. commercial revenue topping government for the first time as businesses adopt more of the company's artificial intelligence tools.
Shares dipped about 3% in extended trading.
Here's how the company did compared to LSEG estimates:
Revenue nearly doubled from a year ago and blew past $2 billion for the first time ever, Palantir said. Net income more than doubled to $1.13 billion, or 44 cents per share, from about $476 million, or 18 cents per share.
"I don't believe anyone's had consistent results like this in the history of software AI, ever," CEO Alex Karp told CNBC's Seema Mody in an interview, adding that the business is succeeding without salespeople.
Palantir has long been known for its strength in the government sector, but its commercial segment caught up in Q3.
U.S. commercial revenue jumped 148% to $984 million, surpassing U.S. government revenue of $953 million, which was up 96%. The company's U.S. commercial revenue has more than quintupled over the last two years.
Palantir lifted its guidance, saying it now expects U.S. commercial revenue "in excess of" $3.56 billion for the full year. Last quarter, the company boosted its forecast to $3.42 billion. The company projects about $2.65 billion in revenue for the fourth quarter and about $8.53 billion for full-year 2026.
Karp has openly supported the use of open-weight models and criticized leading AI labs, which he told CNBC earlier this year are forcing businesses to sell their data sovereignty. Karp, on Monday, also reiterated recent calls to nationalize AI labs, calling it the "only realistic way" to manage liability.
In September, Karp joined major tech CEOs at the White House as calls for regulation mounted following claims from AI researchers that the technology has a more than 10% of killing humanity .
"My message to everybody is: Beware of thinking you can delay the future in AI," he told CNBC. "The future is here. The political ramifications of it are here."

articles.title_orig: 'Quiet quitting' could be hitting the economy - here's why
articles.title_zh: 'Quiet quitting' could be hitting the economy - here's why
articles.content_orig:
The so-called "quiet quitting" trend where workers do the basic requirements of a job but refuse to do anything more might be hitting the economy, analysis has found.
Over the last decade, Britons have become less engaged with the jobs they do and are less willing to put in extra effort, according to a Resolution Foundation report.
The thinktank said this could partly help explain the slump in productivity since the pandemic.
"This is self-evidently bad for workers, but it also doesn't bode well for productivity and labour supply, both of which are vital for lifting living standards in the years ahead," said Hannah Slaughter, principal economist at the Resolution Foundation.
Quiet quitting was popularised on social media shortly after the pandemic .
Frustrated by high demands, low pay, and a squeeze in living standards, many online posts said workers should only do what their bosses asked and nothing more.
So you still show up for work, but no more helping out with additional tasks or checking emails outside work hours, instead focusing on work-life balance and "acting your wage".
Yet, far from being just a talking point on TikTok, the Resolution Foundation said the findings in its report were "consistent" with the idea of quiet quitting.
The percentage of those surveyed willing to go the extra mile to help their employer has sunk from 69% in 2015 to 55% in 2025, according to their survey of 4,656 adults.
Meanwhile, those who were not even "fairly" satisfied with their roles has sunk to one-in-four, the lowest level on record.
In addition, workers are less likely than 10 years ago to say they have an interesting job, with 63% of those surveyed saying so, down from 74%.
"Workers today are indeed a little less committed to their employers, and a little less intrinsically drawn to work in general, than workers were a decade ago," the report added.
This shift over the last decade "may have contributed to weak productivity growth", which has slowed since the financial crisis and weakened again after the pandemic, the Resolution Foundation found.
Workers were also more focused on pay than in the past, which it said was "perhaps unsurprising... given the flatlining living standards of the past decade".
Sir John Curtice, politics professor and co-editor of the report, said the analysis does not mean that young people have "become more 'work-shy', nor have workers in general become more reluctant to change jobs".
"But if workers are to be fully engaged in their work, it has seemingly become more important for employers to provide jobs that are both financially rewarding and have flexible work hours," he added.

Apple Chief Operating Officer Sabih Khan acknowledged the shipping delays plaguing the new iPhone Duo during the company’s fiscal fourth-quarter earnings call on Monday, but offered little clarity on when customers can expect relief.
The delays were just one point of concern during an earnings call filled with questions about the rising costs of memory chips, driven by soaring demand from the AI industry.
“iPhone Duo is constrained as of today. The ramp is going well, and we’re working hard to get this revolutionary new product into the hands of our customers as quickly as possible. But at this time, it’s really hard to predict when supply and demand will be in balance,” Khan said.
Customers who didn’t wait in line at an Apple Store or immediately jump on preorders are now seeing ship times stretch into next year . Meanwhile, Verizon has been apologizing to its customers for the delays by offering gift cards.
In an October report from Financial Times , Apple described demand for the Duo as “nothing short of extraordinary,” after the device sold out on the company’s website within hours of going on sale, pushing delivery dates into next year.
The prolonged shipping delays are notable given Apple’s reputation for its highly efficient supply chain. But the company is hardly alone in facing supply pressures. Soaring demand for memory chips from the AI industry has driven up component costs for hardware makers across the board, threatening to push device prices even higher.
Apple, too, has raised prices on a number of products, Khan noted on the call, adding that those decisions were made “reluctantly.”
In another sign of the company’s efforts to meet demand for the Duo, Apple said it’s “deepening” its partnership with Perryman, a titanium producer for supplying materials for the new foldable device.
“We’ve been thrilled with the early response from reviewers and customers, and we are working hard to get iPhone Duo into customers’ hands as quickly as we can,” Apple CEO John Ternus said during his opening remarks.

articles.title_orig: South of Midnight director says he wouldn’t have funded it if he was Xbox, and he knew ‘Rome would burn’ eventually
articles.title_zh: South of Midnight director says he wouldn’t have funded it if he was Xbox, and he knew ‘Rome would burn’ eventually
articles.content_orig:
The director of South of Midnight says that had he been in Xbox’s position, he wouldn’t have funded the game.
Developed by Canadian studio Compulsion Games , South of Midnight was released for Xbox consoles and PC in April 2025, before coming to PS5 and Switch 2 in March 2026.
The game attracted more than one million players in its first three weeks – a figure which included both sales and players acquiring it through Game Pass.
At the time, Compulsion Games CEO Guillaume Provost said that the studio’s role at Xbox was “not to make blockbusters like Call of Duty, but to provide games that add distinctiveness, where we can either serve audiences that haven’t been served before or create projects that add diversity to the portfolio”.
In July 2026, however Microsoft announced that it was cutting five studios and thousands of jobs as part of its planned business ‘reset’, of which Compulsion Games was one .
Rather than shutting Compulsion down, however, Microsoft agreed a deal to allow to go independent again, and in July the studio announced that it was seeking to collaborate with partners to develop new projects.
Now, in an interview with MinnMax, South of Midnight director David Sears has said that while he appreciated Xbox’s efforts to fund non-mainstream titles to diversify its library, he feels the plan was destined to fail because at some stage a big company will always cut the least profitable parts of the business.
“They were funding a lot of games,” Sears said. “They were also funding a lot of studios that, you know, I was like ‘well, okay, great, I guess you have infinite money, you do you, I want less. I don’t want to feel the weight of the obligation of a giant budget, or an army of 600 to be responsible for. I want to make something that isn’t going to bankrupt Microsoft or the games division.
“So on one hand, if everyone you’re working with is either trying to make generational games at not a huge expense, or games that have huge or really significant contemporary commercial appeal – great, it’s going to work. But when does that ever happen, right?
“In what corporate ecosystem is everyone a good actor – not that anybody’s evil or malicious – but can be counted on to make something that is either going to increase the prestige and the the brand of the studios, or make enough money so that we can make games that increase the prestige and brand, or the reach beyond commercial success?
“There are lots of people who don’t want to play Call of Duty but still love games, and today indies are supplying a lot of that, or helping them scratch that itch.”
Citing the ‘Cassandra complex’ – a term meaning someone who accurately predicts a problem but their warnings are ignored – Sears said he was hopeful that South of Midnight would be a success but believed that eventually Microsoft would stop funding it.
“So yeah, I was like ‘maybe it’s going to be hugely successful, Cassandra would love to be surprised’,” he said. “But she wasn’t! And I literally told people, I was like ‘wow, this could be terrible’, because somebody is going to say one day – you know, the money tap – like, ‘we’re closing those floodgates’, and that’s going to have really traumatic results downstream.”
Sears was asked to clarify whether this meant that while he was thankful for Microsoft’s support, and that South of Midnight’s development had been a positive experience, he would have “turned off the tap” and not funded the game if he had been the one running Xbox.
“Yeah, probably,” he replied. “I mean, I wanted to make it, no doubt, right? Obviously, because we made it. Would I have turned off someone else’s money flow before South of Midnight? Yeah, because I’m not completely selfless.
“But, you know, it just seems like in hindsight at least, it was unsustainable, so of course, it was going to have a shocking outcome.
“It’s easy to dissect it now, but at the time I would talk to other directors and we’d be like: ‘How is this happening? I mean, how did we get so lucky? Is this a golden era?’ And I would always be like ‘for now’.
“There’s always a night when Rome burns,  and I didn’t know exactly when it would be, but I was always worried about it.”
“There’s always a night when Rome burns,  and I didn’t know exactly when it would be, but I was always worried about it.”
Sears left Compulsion in March 2025, so he wasn’t around when Microsoft subsequently decided to cut ties with the studio, but he praised it for giving Compulsion the chance to go indie again instead of simply shutting it down, citing its previous acquisition of Age of Empires studio Ensemble in 2001 and its closure in 2009.
“To their credit, amazing… I think there’s a definitely a corporate Microsoft DNA, but they are vastly different from the Microsoft I knew back in the ’90s or the early 2000s. Much more humane, actually.
“It’s remarkable and commendable, and the fact they didn’t do what their predecessors might have done – remember when they bought Ensemble and it was like ‘oh my God, we’re gonna have a infinite number of Age of Empires!’ No, no.
“But now they’ve let studios spin off, right? Compulsion, I believe, is indie now. And what a ride, right? They went from, a very small start-up independent to fully owned by Microsoft with a great studio that we didn’t get to use enough, to now being independent again.”

articles.title_orig: Deadly RSF drone attacks reveal deep divisions between Sudan and Ethiopia
articles.title_zh: Deadly RSF drone attacks reveal deep divisions between Sudan and Ethiopia
articles.content_orig:
The Sudanese government’s allegations that Ethiopia is behind a deadly wave of unmanned aerial assaults belie a deep and longstanding rift between the two countries, which threatens to intensify internal conflicts in both.
Sudan has officially lodged complaints with the United Nations Security Council and the African Union’s Peace and Security Council over allegations that the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) paramilitary – which has been at war with the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) since April 2023 – is using Ethiopian territory to launch attacks against civilian sites, including power stations.
Ethiopia’s alleged support for the RSF has triggered differences within the SAF on how to respond next, Sudanese border affairs specialist Abdul Kareem Al-Almin Ahmed told Al Jazeera.
“The mutual accusations are many and almost daily, and the tension on the part of the Sudanese army has reached high levels, to the degree that made some voices inside the Sudanese army and the forces allied with it demand that Sudan declare war on Ethiopia based on these interventions,” Al-Almin told Al Jazeera.
Suspected RSF drone attacks have heavily damaged civilian infrastructure in SAF-controlled areas. More than 90 percent of power stations in Sudanese cities have been rendered out of service due to drone attacks, and al-Almin said the technological capabilities of these weapons indicate significant external backing.
“They are mysterious drones, drones that reach long distances, and almost all Sudanese lands are currently violated by these drones, which confirms that they are drones with a special characteristic and flight properties for a long range and have high destructive power,” Al-Almin added.
A detailed report prepared by the Sudanese Ministry of Foreign Affairs alongside military intelligence claimed that 70 separate assaults involving 187 one-way attack drones were launched from Ethiopian territory between February and October. The frequency of these attacks seems to be increasing, with 28 attacks carried out by 97 drones in October.
The use of armed drones has been catastrophic for civilians in Sudan, with 13 million people already displaced and thousands at risk of famine due to the war.
Between February 15 and October 27, drone attacks killed 176 Sudanese soldiers and 484 civilians, according to a report compiled by the Transitional Sovereignty Council, which is linked to the de facto Sudanese leader Abdel Fattah al-Burhan and the SAF. It identified Asosa Airport in western Ethiopia, the Kurmuk-Gizen border area, and the Bahir Dar airbase in Amhara as specific launch sites for drone attacks.
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said on Saturday he was appalled by the use of drones in the war and condemned the catastrophic toll this was having on civilians. A drone attack on displaced families in Wad el-Mahi , near the Ethiopian border on October 3, killed 26 women and four children. Another drone attack in Nyala, in Sudan’s Darfur region, on October 26 killed at least 21 people and injured at least 40.
The Sudanese military has repeatedly accused the Ethiopian government of aiding the RSF. Addis Ababa denies the claims and has in turn accused the Sudanese government of backing rebels linked to the Tigray People’s Liberation Front .
The tensions between Sudan and Ethiopia extend beyond these drone attacks and allegations of support for rebel groups. They also involve a confrontation over water resources and strategic regional alliances.
There have been ongoing tensions between Sudan and Ethiopia over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD), built by Addis Ababa on the Nile River.
Egypt and Sudan rely heavily on the Nile for water supplies and, being downstream, fear the GERD threatens their national security and claim it breaches international law.
“The Sudanese-Ethiopian file is a complex file, in which many factors have intertwined: The Renaissance Dam problem first … and the rapprochement between the Sudanese army and the Egyptian government,” Al-Almin said. The Sudanese government is also angered that the RSF is allegedly receiving support from Ethiopia, he added.
But Badr Hassan Al-Shafei, a professor of African studies and conflict resolution expert, said fears of an escalation that could harm Sudan and Ethiopia are preventing an all-out confrontation between the two countries.
In a study published by the Al Jazeera Centre for Studies, Al-Shafei wrote that “Khartoum’s interest lies in the stability of its eastern neighbourhood to avoid security threats and waves of asylum.
“Khartoum fears that providing military support to Tigray will lead to an explosion of the situation on its borders, which may increase displacement operations that the border Sudanese states cannot bear, especially in light of the continuation of the war against Hemedti,” Al-Shafei stated.
A direct military confrontation with Addis Ababa would severely strain an already exhausted Sudanese military apparatus, which is still involved in intense battles with the RSF in the southeast of the country.
Ultimately, leaders of both countries recognise the catastrophic potential of expanding the battlefield beyond each other’s borders.
“If the Sudanese army opens a war front with Ethiopia, this is not in its favour and confuses the region,” Al-Amin wrote.
“[Sudan could find itself] fighting on two fronts: Fighting the Rapid Support Forces that occupy part of Sudan, and fighting the Ethiopian army that possesses its capabilities and the border extension capable of reaching through it.”

articles.title_orig: As Trump’s Midterm Deadline Looms, Gulf Countries Brace for Possible Renewal of Iran War
articles.title_zh: As Trump’s Midterm Deadline Looms, Gulf Countries Brace for Possible Renewal of Iran War
articles.content_orig:
Some Arab states have warned Iran that they could retaliate individually or collectively if Tehran targets their infrastructure, as Persian Gulf countries prepare for the possibility of renewed US strikes and Iranian retaliation, the Wall Street Journal reported Monday.
Qatar and the United Arab Emirates have been conducting security drills, including at airports, while some attendees at a major energy conference in Abu Dhabi were cutting short their stays on government advice. Schools in Riyadh were also set to remain online this week as Saudi Arabia faces attacks by the Iran-backed Houthis. UAE presidential adviser Anwar Gargash said his country hoped diplomatic efforts would succeed but was “braced for the worst.”
The warnings come against a backdrop of continuing attacks around the Strait of Hormuz. A tanker was struck by two unidentified projectiles near a Saudi port late Sunday, while another vessel was hit by an unidentified projectile off Oman early Monday. Iranian state media also reported Monday that an oil tanker caught fire after striking a mine in the eastern part of the strait.
The heightened preparations coincide with diplomatic efforts to prevent renewed fighting. Iranian negotiators left Doha on Sunday, with a draft proposal still circulating for feedback and a follow-up meeting possible. An Iranian source cited by the IRGC-affiliated Fars news agency said Monday that indirect communications with Washington had produced no diplomatic breakthrough and that Tehran continued to insist on its seven conditions. A third Qatari delegation in a week was heading to Tehran on Monday as Doha sought to bring Tehran and Washington closer to an agreement to end the war, Al-Araby Al-Jadeed reported, citing an informed Iranian source.
Axios reported that Qatari mediators had drafted an agreement outlining a three-day sequence of confidence-building measures aimed at resuming direct US-Iran negotiations. Trump told Axios he was “in no rush” to decide whether to resume fighting with Iran, saying: “One way or the other, we will do something, but there is no rush.” The diplomatic push has also exposed differing views within the Trump administration over how to proceed. CIA Director John Ratcliffe, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Secretary of State Marco Rubio favor maintaining economic pressure without either a new war or a deal, while Vice President JD Vance and White House envoy Steve Witkoff are urging Trump to move toward an agreement, Axios reported.
Vance said Monday that Washington had made “some progress” toward a negotiated settlement. “The President and I both feel pretty good about the prospects for potentially coming to a negotiated settlement,” Vance said, adding: “We've certainly made some progress. We'll see if we can make some more.”
Despite those signs of progress, the possibility of renewed US military action remains. The Journal reported that Trump has been leaning toward a large attack on Iran after the US midterm election but has not decided whether to proceed. Trump told Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in a call Saturday that he wanted to first give continuing diplomatic efforts a chance to succeed, according to people familiar with the call.
“Prime Minister Netanyahu is not pressing President Trump. President Trump knows exactly what he wants to achieve and how he wants to achieve it,” Danny Danon told Al Arabiya English.
“Israel will collaborate with the United States. We will support the decision of the United States, but it is not us pressing anyone,” he added.
Danon’s remarks followed an Axios report Sunday, citing an Israeli and a US source, that Netanyahu was urging Trump to strike Iran immediately after the November 3 elections, while the US president preferred to allow negotiations to continue.
The Israeli source described the leaders’ Saturday phone call as “tough,” while the US source called it “direct.”
Trump confirmed Sunday that he had spoken with Netanyahu about Iran, describing their conversation as “a very good talk,” without providing further details.
Danon also rejected a claim by US commentator Tucker Carlson on X that a nuclear strike against Iran was being considered, calling the idea “delusional.”
“No one is even discussing it in the US, nor in Israel,” he said.
Washington weighs military options and diplomacy
Trump said Saturday that negotiations with Iran were “going fine” and that he was in no hurry to resume military action, although he said Washington still needed to target one or two sites, including the suspected underground nuclear complex at Pickaxe Mountain.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Saturday that Trump had not decided whether to launch further strikes.
“He hasn’t made a decision,” Rubio told reporters in Atlanta, adding that Washington preferred to resolve the conflict peacefully.
Rubio said diplomatic contacts had remained active, often through intermediaries, and declined to set a deadline for negotiations.
Iran says diplomatic contacts remain active
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Monday that consultations through mediators, including Qatar and Pakistan, remained intensive, after several days of talks with Qatari officials ended without a breakthrough.
“Everything depends on the political rationality of Washington,” Araghchi said, according to the state-run IRNA news agency.
Araghchi said a revised proposal developed through mediation could allow the Strait of Hormuz to reopen within two days if Washington accepts Iran’s conditions.
Tehran’s earlier seven-day plan called for Washington to lift its blockade of Iranian ports, release frozen Iranian assets and waive sanctions on Iranian oil sales before negotiations resumed.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian also said Monday that Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei had granted the government “certain authorities” regarding peace talks with the United States, according to IRNA.
Pezeshkian said Iran would seek to resolve the conflict through dialogue, without specifying the scope of those powers.
An Iranian source cited by the Revolutionary Guards-affiliated Fars news agency said Monday that indirect communications with Washington had produced no breakthrough and that Tehran still insisted on its seven conditions for progress. Exchanging messages through intermediaries was routine, the source said.
Despite the diplomatic contacts, Danon said in his Monday interview that Israel remained prepared for military action regardless of uncertainty surrounding the formation of a new government following last week’s Israeli elections.
“The military is prepared, we are ready and if we will need to protect our people, we will do it,” he said.
The country’s dependence on the waterway leaves its gas industry exposed to prolonged shipping disruptions. For state-owned QatarEnergy, buying supplies produced outside the Persian Gulf offers a way to earn trading income when its own exports are constrained.
The new contracts will begin delivering in 2030 or later. They offer protection against future losses, but cannot restore shipments from Qatar’s damaged facilities or reopen its export route.
The risks were underscored on Friday, when a Qatari LNG carrier was struck by “unidentified objects” in the Persian Gulf, the same day Qatari mediators held talks in Tehran aimed at reaching a deal between Iran and the United States.
The Al Mayeda was hit Friday evening, its owner Nakilat said Sunday. No crew members were injured or environmental damage reported, and the vessel remained operational.
Qatar condemned the attack as a “dangerous act” threatening maritime navigation and global energy supplies, saying investigations were underway to identify those responsible.
War exposes Qatar’s dependence on Hormuz
Qatar is particularly vulnerable to disruption in the Strait of Hormuz. LNG accounts for half of its foreign-currency export revenues, and shipments to markets beyond the Persian Gulf must pass through the waterway.

articles.title_orig: Iran warns of ‘new battlefield’ after reported US strike on Qeshm
articles.title_zh: Iran warns of ‘new battlefield’ after reported US strike on Qeshm
articles.content_orig:
Iran's parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf warned on Tuesday that any US strategic error would open "a new battlefield in the war," hours after a US Air Force jet reportedly struck an IRGC missile system on Qeshm Island.
Ghalibaf told parliament Iran was at its highest level of defensive readiness, and that responsibility for preventing further escalation rested with Washington. "The ball is in America's court to prevent war," he said.
The remarks came after residents of Qeshm Island, Hengam and Bandar Abbas reported successive explosions and tremors overnight, according to Iranian news agencies IRNA and Fars.
US media outlets reported that a US Air Force jet had struck an IRGC surface-to-air missile launch system on the island after a missile had been fired from Qeshm at a US aircraft in the Strait of Hormuz.
The operation was described as limited and aimed at protecting commercial shipping. CENTCOM issued no formal statement confirming or denying the accounts, and no Iranian military or government official formally confirmed a direct attack on the island.
The IRGC said separately that its electronic warfare systems had downed two US MQM-170 reconnaissance drones south of Qeshm Island and destroyed a US MQ-9 drone east of the Strait of Hormuz.
Ghalibaf said late Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, as commander-in-chief, had defined Iran's military strategy for confronting a possible attack.
According to Ghalibaf, senior military commanders and Mojtaba Khamenei — the new supreme leader in direct control of the IRGC — met last week and reportedly decided on "a response without geographical limits" and Tehran's right to determine when any conflict ends.
Former foreign minister and parliamentarian Manouchehr Mottaki said on Sunday he interpreted that formulation to mean US military bases in European countries, including Britain, Italy, Portugal and Germany, could be drawn into any conflict. "If our war is to break out, it will no longer be a regional war, it will be extraregional," he said.
Tehran-based Hamshahri newspaper reported on Tuesday that Iran had updated its "target bank," examining a scenario in which US support bases and infrastructure in Europe would be targeted under the "response without geographical limits" strategy.
Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi expressed support for Gulf state mediation in a post on X. "We have no hostility with the Gulf Cooperation Council countries, we value the positive role played by Qatar and Oman, and we continue dialogue with Saudi Arabia," he said.

articles.title_orig: Smugglers Bypass U.S. Controls to Ship HBM to China
articles.title_zh: Smugglers Bypass U.S. Controls to Ship HBM to China
articles.content_orig:
Despite U.S. export controls on advanced semiconductors to China, High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) produced by Samsung Electronics and SK hynix is reportedly being smuggled into China. Smugglers are using a method of packaging HBMs with low-end server processors to bypass export regulations, and then detaching only the memory once in China.
According to the U.S. IT media outlet The Information on Nov. 2 (local time), smugglers who have recently been siphoning Korean HBMs to China are exploiting loopholes in export regulations.
They package the HBM with a low-end server processor on a board and export it to China. They target the fact that while exporting HBM alone is subject to U.S. regulations, packaging it with a server processor classifies the package as a server processor item.
Under U.S. export regulations, the total computing power of a semiconductor package is evaluated based on the server processor, not the memory chip. The packages are disassembled upon arriving in China. Local technicians apply heat to the board to melt the solder, detach only the necessary HBM, and discard the remaining server processors.
The separation process requires highly sophisticated skills. It is reported that the failure rate is high because applying heat too quickly or for an extended period can cause the memory stack to warp or crack.
Nevertheless, the smuggling continues due to the massive profits.
A broker in his 20s who handles HBM smuggling in China told The Information that the price of a single HBM3E, which traded for several hundred dollars just a year ago, has recently soared to about $4,000. A single AI chip package requires 6 to 8 HBMs. The memory price alone amounts to $24,000 to $32,000. AI processors, servers, and power costs are separate.
The HBMs secured in this way are reportedly sold mainly to customers of Huawei, a Chinese telecommunications equipment and IT company.
According to sources familiar with Huawei’s supply chain, Huawei recently explained to some customers that its next-generation flagship AI chip, the Ascend 960DT, will largely be equipped with HBMs produced by Samsung Electronics and SK hynix. Huawei introduced that the performance of the Ascend 960DT is twice as superior as existing chips, and it will be one of the powerful processors that China can produce on its own.
As it became difficult to directly purchase the necessary memory chips from Korean companies, Huawei even advised some AI chip ordering customers to secure HBMs on their own. China is clinging to securing Korean HBMs because it lacks its own production capacity.
HBM is a core component that enhances the processing performance of AI processors by quickly transmitting large amounts of data. Without securing enough HBMs, it is difficult for a high-performance AI chip to exert its full performance even if it is developed. Samsung Electronics and SK hynix account for more than 80% of the global HBM market.
The problem is that such smuggling could also act as a burden on Korean semiconductor companies. Even if Samsung Electronics and SK hynix did not directly violate export control regulations, they could become targets of U.S. government surveillance if Chinese AI chips equipped with their memory are discovered.
In fact, Taiwan’s TSMC was investigated by the U.S. government in 2024 after semiconductors it produced were found in Huawei products. Subsequently, the U.S. ordered TSMC to completely halt AI chip exports to China.
SK hynix stated, “We are strictly complying with relevant laws and regulations, including the export control regulations of the U.S. and South Korea,” adding that it has never supplied products to Huawei since the implementation of U.S. export regulations in 2020.
Meanwhile, a perception is emerging among smugglers who consider their transactions to be a patriotic act.
A broker in his 20s who smuggles memory in China told The Information regarding his work, “It is contributing to the motherland.” He reportedly does not consider himself a smuggler.
However, as smuggling competition intensifies, concerns about crackdowns are also growing.
Another smuggler who has been ordering memory semiconductors from South Korea revealed that the risk of detection is increasing as other brokers have started using the transaction routes he used.
He said, “The more people like us there are, the easier it becomes to be discovered by regulatory authorities,” adding that he plans to sell most of his company stakes next year as crackdowns by South Korea and the U.S. are expected to be further strengthened in the future.

articles.content_orig:
Fox News chief foreign correspondent Trey Yingst reports on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's response to Russian attacks, warning that strikes on their infrastructure will meet a painful response.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned Monday that Russia is preparing a "massive attack" on Ukraine centered on Tuesday's midterm elections in the United States, accusing Moscow of seeking to exploit the historical vote to unleash strikes while the world's attention is elsewhere.
The Ukrainian leader's warning came as voters prepared to decide which party controls Congress, a result that could also influence Washington's future response to Russian President Vladimir Putin's almost five-year war in Ukraine.
In a post on X, Zelenskyy went on to urge the Trump administration to increase pressure on Moscow, warning that Russia could exploit the elections to target Ukraine's battered energy infrastructure and supply routes.
DRONE STRIKE SINKS SHIP IN NATO WATERS AS ZELENSKYY WARNS OF LOOMING ‘MASSIVE STRIKE’
Russian President Vladimir Putin and Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. (Vyacheslav Prokofyev/Sputnik/Kremlin Pool Photo/Efrem Lukatsky/AP)
"We have intel that Russia is preparing a new massive attack on our country – primarily targeting energy and logistics," Zelenskyy said in his nightly address.
"The assumption is basically that tomorrow the world will be watching the American midterms, and what is happening here in Ukraine, along with our difficulties with air defense and Patriot missiles, will be overlooked."
Zelenskyy's warning came hours after Russian forces struck a school being used to distribute humanitarian aid in Komyshuvakha, a settlement in southeastern Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia region.
At least 26 people, including police officers and first responders, were killed, five others were injured and others remained missing, according to the Ukrainian news outlet Ukrainska Pravda .
ZELENSKYY PRESSURES US AND EUROPE FOR MORE 'AIR DEFENSE' ASSISTANCE AMID ONGOING WAR WITH RUSSIA
Ukraine's largest private energy company reports 90% of generation capacity damaged by Russian attacks, leaving over 1 million without power during freezing temperatures. (Reuters)
In his X post, Zelenskyy urged the U.S. and its allies to warn Putin that continued attacks on Ukraine would bring serious economic consequences.
"We need signals from the world to Russia that will make them feel that terror is no good, that it will bring no gains, and that as long as this war continues, their oil will burn, and they will not be able to make money doing business with the world," Zelenskyy warned.
"We must not play games with Russia's oil or gas revenues," he added.
"We must put pressure on Russia in such a way that it has no alternative but to end this war. America can do this."
TRUMP ANNOUNCES IMMEDIATE ENERGY CEASEFIRE BETWEEN RUSSIA AND UKRAINE
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, left talks with President Donald Trump and members of his Cabinet during a lunch meeting at the White House on Oct. 17, 2025, in Washington, D.C. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)
President Donald Trump, meanwhile, has sought to negotiate an end to the war with the help of special envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner , both of whom have been involved in diplomatic efforts with Moscow.
Zelenskyy told Fox News in a Sunday interview that Ukraine would suspend strikes on Russian oil refineries for a month if Washington provided Patriot missile interceptors during the same period, potentially opening the door to diplomacy.
The State Department approved the potential sale of 500 Patriot PAC-3 interceptor missiles to Ukraine for an estimated $2.1 billion, according to Reuters.

Ukraine's General Staff accused Russian forces of using the humanitarian pause to rotate troops, reinforce their defenses and improve battlefield logistics.

articles.content_orig:
Those travelling from Hangzhou or Wuhan can have bags checked through to final destination overseas under new one-stop service launched on Tuesday
Travellers flying from Hangzhou or Wuhan to overseas destinations via Hong Kong on different airlines can have their baggage checked through to the final destination under a newly launched service that aims to step up the connections between mainland Chinese cities and other countries.
Under the new one-stop service that launched on Tuesday, travellers departing from Hangzhou Xiaoshan International Airport or Wuhan Tianhe International Airport will not need to check in their baggage again when transferring through Hong Kong, even if they are flying on a different airline on the next leg of their journey.
“Hong Kong International Airport is launching a game-changing service,” Secretary for Transport and Logistics Mable Chan said.

articles.title_orig: Asian trading is mixed as tech sell-off deepens and oil prices rebound
articles.title_zh: Asian trading is mixed as tech sell-off deepens and oil prices rebound
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Oil prices tumbled more than seven percent on Monday, the eve of crucial midterm elections in the United States, as signals that Tehran and Washington were renewing dialogue boosted hopes of ending the Middle East war.
Iran on Monday said "intensive" exchanges were underway with Washington and offered to reopen the Strait of Hormuz under strict conditions, as efforts escalated to avert a return to conflict.
Earlier, the Axios news outlet reported that US Vice President JD Vance had sent a letter to Iranian national security chief Mohsen Rezaei about possible new talks.
That was the highest-level move from President Donald Trump's administration in months.
Again Capital's John Kilduff described investors as experiencing "a violent change in market sentiment," adding that "we went from really, I think, expecting a major offensive after tomorrow's US elections to a potential breakthrough," he told AFP.
"All these losses will be taken right back if this doesn't pan out," Kilduff said.
The steep drop in oil prices translated into weakness among petroleum stocks. But Wall Street shares otherwise began the day with promise, bouncing back after last Friday's rout precipitated by worries over the tech industry's massive artificial intelligence spending.
But tech shares came under pressure as the session progressed, with the tech-focused Nasdaq slumping 1.1 percent.
"This is still a market that is on edge," said Joseph Zidle, chief market strategist at Cresset Capital, who described unease about midterm elections as adding to worries about the AI boom.
"The two of them are actually related," Zidle said of midterms and AI, noting that opposition to data centers has animated many campaigns.
AI has been "on the ballot in so many places, both blue and red," Zidle said. "It seems like data centers are part of the kitchen table issues."
Pollsters expect Democrats to win back control of the House of Representatives, but view Trump's Republican party as potentially able to maintain a majority in the Senate.
The loss of total Republican dominance would push the president into unfamiliar and uncomfortable territory: a lame duck period beset with high inflation at home, the sputtering war against Iran and hostile Democratic investigations into his activities in Washington.
"Investors are bracing for a fresh round of turbulence ahead of US midterm election fireworks while they assess the extent that companies are burning through cash to keep the AI bonfires burning," said Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at Wealth Club.
Earnings this week will come from Apple, which reports after the close of trading on Monday, as well as Advanced Micro Devices and software titan Palantir will be closely watched this week. Shares in Apple fell 1.8 percent.

articles.title_orig: Blackstone president calls for more equity to fund AI buildout as debt risks mount
articles.title_zh: Blackstone president calls for more equity to fund AI buildout as debt risks mount
articles.content_orig:
The artificial intelligence infrastructure buildout will need more equity financing as lenders become increasingly exposed to the companies driving the buildout, Blackstone President Jon Gray said Tuesday.
Speaking at the Hong Kong Monetary Authority’s Global Financial Leaders’ Investment Summit, Gray said the scale of capital required for AI is creating concentration risks for debt investors, both across the sector and at individual companies.
Unlike shareholders, who can benefit from a company's growth, lenders have limited upside as their returns are largely confined to interest and principal repayments, he said.
Speaking at the same panel, Pimco CEO Emmanuel Roman warned investors that the scale of AI financing could prove to be "too much" for markets to absorb.
Roman said AI-related capital spending could reach around $10 trillion over the next five years, citing General Atlantic CEO Bill Ford's estimate. He added that about $550 billion in AI debt had been issued in various forms so far this year.
Even with a mix of equity and debt financing, the amount required would be “gigantic,” Roman said, comparing it with a global corporate bond market of roughly $20 trillion.
“At some point in time, it’s going to be too much,” he said.
Global data center demand will require about $8.5 trillion in capital spending over the next five years, Goldman Sachs wrote in a report Monday.
Gray said financing the buildout would require a combination of public markets, banks and private capital, with companies increasingly turning to structured transactions to limit the amount of debt they take on. Cash generated by hyperscalers would also fund part of the spending, he said.
“The creativity is needed because the scale of capital is enormous," Gray said.
Despite those financing challenges, Gray remained bullish on AI infrastructure, saying demand for computing power was “running well ahead of supply.”
Spending on AI models across Blackstone’s portfolio companies had risen 20-fold over the past year as businesses saw financial benefits from uses including coding, customer engagement and content creation, he said.
Meeting that demand remains difficult, however, as securing sites, permits, chips, power and capital becomes more challenging, according to Gray.

articles.title_orig: North Korea denies being behind $6.3bn Binance crypto hack
articles.title_zh: North Korea denies being behind $6.3bn Binance crypto hack
articles.content_orig:
North Korea has denied claims that it was behind the record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) hack of cryptocurrency exchange Binance , calling the allegations "absurd rhetoric".
Kim Yo Jong, a top Democratic People's Republic of Korea official and the sister of leader Kim Jong Un , said on Tuesday that the accusations are another "sinister attempt" by the US to damage Pyongyang's public image.
The US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), the Secret Service and cyber analysts have said North Korea orchestrated the hack, which has been described as the largest in history.
This is the latest hack to be linked to North Korea, which has been accused of relying on cyber-crime to help finance its sanctioned economy.
Blockchain analysts and the FBI have said the attack was led by state-backed hacking group TraderTraitor.
The FBI has called on industry partners to help block transactions involving cryptocurrency accounts linked to the group.
"The US has made a trite provocation of linking it with the Democratic People's Republic of Korea again," Kim Yo-jong, the director of North Korea's General Affairs Department, said in a statement.
"It is a grave political provocation against the DPRK that the US misleads the international public opinion as if all the cyber crimes in different parts of the world are our deeds," she said.
But Pyongyang has been blamed for a number of major cyber attacks in recent years - accusations that it has denied.
The TraderTraitor unit, which is also known as the Lazarus Group, was blamed for a then-record $1.5bn hack of crypto exchange Bybit in 2025.
Pyongyang has systematically built its cyber operations, recruiting promising students from universities and sending them to hacker units overseen by North Korea's intelligence agency, research groups like the S Rajaratnam School of International Studies think tank have said.
The country has consistently denied such claims.
Kim Yo Jong said "it is the consistent policy stand of the DPRK government to resolutely oppose all sorts of malicious acts in cyberspace".
Binance did not respond to the BBC's queries about North Korea's alleged involvement in the hack.
Since the incident, the crypto giant has largely focused its public statements on the technical nature of the breach and its response to protect users.
The company's spokesperson said that a net $4.72bn has been withdrawn from the exchange since transactions resumed on Sunday.
The net outflow represents a "relatively limited portion"  of Binance's total assets, which stand at approximately $157bn, the spokesperson told the BBC on Tuesday.
That figure reflects the impact of the hack, subsequent withdrawals and market price changes.
"Withdrawal levels are stabilising to what we would consider normal and expected on-chain activity," she added.
The company said last week that initial checks indicated that an engineer's laptop had been compromised, enabling an attacker to make unauthorised withdrawals.
Trading in major cryptocurrencies on Binance has since resumed after the exchange worked with issuers to freeze assets impacted by the hack.
The company has repeatedly said it would cover all of the losses linked to the attack and that it has so far covered around 95% of the assets stolen in the breach.

articles.title_orig: Jeffrey Sachs On Economy, Ties With China & New World Order (Transcript)
articles.title_zh: Jeffrey Sachs On Economy, Ties With China & New World Order (Transcript)
articles.content_orig:
In this keynote at the Aristotle-Confucius Symposium in Varanasi, economist Jeffrey Sachs traces how Asia’s share of world production fell under European and American imperialism and why it is now returning to the center of the global economy. He talks about India-China ties, the rise of a multipolar world, family businesses and corporate responsibility, reviving the United Nations, and why the shared ethics of the world’s great traditions can help build a new world order of peace and cooperation. Read the full transcript of this lecture below:
JEFFREY SACHS: Good morning, friends. Doctor Adani, thank you for that brilliant address, but especially for all that you and your family and the foundation are doing for the world, which is very profound and very moving also to hear. And, Nirupam, thank you for the last thirty two years of collaboration and the continuing thirty two years of collaboration at least. I’m thrilled with all that we do together and most grateful. I want to thank the government of India, the Ministry of Culture.
I know the Secretary of Culture will be arriving shortly. His plane was diverted because of the fog this morning, but I think he’s landed and will arrive soon. I want to thank the partnership, of course, of the Adani Foundation and the Adani Group. And to pay my great respect to what the Adani Group is doing for sustainable development in India and globally because the scale of your work is remarkable as you just described, and it’s very, very inspiring. I’d like to thank TERI, which is a partner in organizing this symposium.
With TERI, we go back many decades of TERI’s leadership in sustainable development and in green energy and in climate safety. So it’s a tremendous joy to be working with TERI and joining together with TERI.
For me, it’s very moving to be here in Varanasi. Sonia and I first came here forty seven years ago. We fell in love with this magical place, which is one of the great, most holy places on the planet and one of the greatest centers of learning and knowledge and spirituality in the world, there’s probably not another place that combines such crucial world traditions as the place where we are.
So to be in Varanasi is absolutely extraordinary. We keep coming back, and we are inspired every time that we come together. And for me, it’s wonderful that so many of our colleagues and friends from this effort of ancient wisdom for modern challenges are together again here so that we can add, I think, significantly and profoundly to the depth of our work together and to help advance that work.
I’d like to spend a few minutes on the background of this symposium and why I think it’s so important. I have prepared remarks, which I will share with anyone that’s interested later, but I will not read them certainly right now.
I want to just share some basic thoughts with you. And I do need one slide, this one. So a lot of numbers, but the numbers… I’m an economist. I can’t help but look at some numbers.
But the numbers, I think, are absolutely key to understanding our world today. We are in a new territory in the world, not only because of AI or because of climate change or because of other technological disruptions that we face or being in the nuclear age, which is sad to say, perhaps the deepest reality of our world, which is the capacity to… Of humanity to end humanity in about seventy minutes as the current analyses show.
But we’re in a different world because history has moved in a very important and fundamental way, and that’s what these numbers help us to understand. So what you see here for several benchmark years starting in 1700 at the top row and then going to projections to 2100 to the end of the twenty first century in the bottom row, our estimates of the share of world production, this is a shorthand, but the share of the world product produced in different regions of the world.
And I’m showing you The United States, Europe, which in this case is the European Union plus Great Britain, China, and India. And I want you to see what has happened in history and what is happening today. Back in 1700, China and India each had about 20% of world production. Europe, about 24%. The United States didn’t exist yet.
It wouldn’t exist till the end of the example very to see be so of how that we’re world. The world economy. There’s obviously other places of not counted in this table to add up to a 100%.
As late as 1800, China was a third of world output more than Europe. India had already started to lose its share because India was already starting to be imperialized by Britain and by other European empires, which would be soon kicked out by Britain.
But India was being held back by the British Empire. China, not yet. It had not faced yet British imperialism that was to come starting in 1839. The United States now existed, and it was 1% of world output.
By 1900, the world had changed fundamentally because the nineteenth century was the century in which Europe temporarily dominated the world, and that was the world of European empire, not centuries long a century of domination of the nineteenth century.
And in that nineteenth century, of course, India fell entirely under British rule. China entered into what China calls the “century of humiliation,” which began with the… One of the most sordid wars of history, the war by Britain on China to force China to open up to actually British grown, India grown opium. It’s hard to imagine a more disgusting war than this, although I think the current Iran war ranks high as well, a war out of nothing.
But the Opium Wars started a century of disaster for China because two Opium Wars were followed by a massive civil war in China after those disruptions, known to us as the Taiping Rebellion, but really one of the largest civil wars in history.
And to cap that off at the end of the nineteenth century, Japan invaded China and began forty years of invasions of China so that there was catastrophe in both India and China.
Millions of people died in repeated famines in India completely unrelieved by the British Empire who stuck with a stiff upper lip to their laissez faire policy as people were dying and continued to export grains from famine stricken regions of this country.
So by 1900, Europe’s share of the world output was almost 40%. China and India together, and, of course, India being part of the British empire at that point, were now less than 20%.
So a decline to a mere 18% of world output for two countries that held more than 40% of the world population. 1950 was the nadir of Asia because this was a hundred fifty years of European and then American imperialism with American overseas imperialism starting in the eighteen nineties, first overthrowing the Kingdom of Hawaii and then taking the colony of The Philippines in the so called Spanish-American War.
Look at the situation in 1950. 56% of world output was in The United States and Europe, more than half. Whereas in China and India now combined on the independence of India and the independence of the People’s Republic Of China under 10% combined for two countries which still constituted more than 40% of world output.
That world of 1950 and the world that was created between 1800 and 1950 came to be seen as the norm of the world, that the West leads the world, the West designs the global realities, Asia is a small footnote under Western guidance, and this ideology was the prevailing ideology of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. It’s the ideology that I grew up in myself and that I was trained in.
When I… When Sonia and I came to India in 1979, I was enthralled. This was a completely new world, an impoverished world, and I carried in my backpack a famous book of the time called “Asian Drama” by Gunnar Myrdal, which explained to me why Asia was poor and will always be poor.
This was the basic lesson of the “Asian Drama.” He won a Nobel Prize, certainly not for that. Most Nobel Prizes in economics are wrong anyway, but that one

articles.title_orig: UK to double wait for permanent residency, with exemptions for care workers
articles.title_zh: UK to double wait for permanent residency, with exemptions for care workers
articles.content_orig:
Al Jazeera investigation exposes paramilitary hitman linked to Turning Point UK
The United Kingdom has revised its immigration rules, doubling the time most foreign workers must wait to qualify for permanent residency to 10 years and making refugees who arrive on “small boats” wait as long as 30 years.
Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood, speaking in Parliament on Monday, said hundreds of thousands of care workers will be exempt from the hardline rules, offering a concession amid a political outcry within the governing Labour Party.
Permanent residency, known in the UK as indefinite leave to remain, carries the right to work, study, use the free National Health Service and claim welfare benefits. Until now, it has been granted after five years.
The new rules, set to take effect next year, tie eligibility for permanent residency to income.
People who earn more than 50,000 pounds a year ($67,000) will still be able to apply after five years, and those earning more than 125,000 pounds ($167,500) after three. Everyone else will be placed on the 10-year path. The median salary in the UK is about 39,000 pounds (roughly $52,000).
The rules will apply retroactively to workers already in the country.
“Settlement should not be automatic. It should be earned,” Mahmood, the home secretary, told Parliament, adding that the changes would restore fairness by linking the right to settle to what immigrants contribute.
“Those who contribute most will settle fastest,” she said. “Those who don’t play by the rules will be refused or wait longer.”
The UK government first proposed last year that lower-skilled workers wait 10 to 15 years for permanent residency.
But the plan drew fierce opposition from unions and parts of the Labour Party, particularly over its effect on care workers, who are often poorly paid and work in a sector that has long struggled to fill vacancies. Many of them arrived in the early 2020s, as the country was reeling from the COVID-19 pandemic, to fill gaps left by European workers who had departed after Brexit.
Under the revised plan, care workers will be able to settle after five years if they have met the conditions of their visas and earn at least 25,000 pounds ($33,500) a year.
Mahmood said the rules would offer a path for care workers “who worked hard and answered our call when we needed them”.
As for refugees, those who arrive through one of the government’s “new safe and legal routes” will be able to settle after five years, she said. For other refugees, the standard wait will become 20 years, reduced to 10 years for those who work or study. Anyone who arrived by an “illegal method”, such as by small boat, could wait up to 30 years for settlement, she said.
Under the new rules, applicants will also be disqualified if they have a criminal record, cannot speak English “to a high standard”, owe money to the government, or have not made at least three years of national insurance contributions.
Mahmood said the overhaul would mean that half a million people would settle later than they otherwise would have, saving the government billions of pounds in benefits.
In total, the government estimates that as many as 1.4 million people will receive settled status between 2026 and 2030.
The changes, announced after a 12-week public consultation that drew more than 200,000 responses, are part of a broader effort to tighten immigration rules after arrivals surged following Brexit.
They are a response to political pressure, including from Nigel Farage’s populist Reform UK party, which has surged in popularity in recent years with calls for stricter migration controls. Reform UK has sought to depict the arrivals of refugees on small boats across the English Channel as a crisis, and anti-immigration activists have staged protests, including outside facilities that house asylum seekers.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s government has said that increased law enforcement cooperation between the UK and France has helped reduce the number of people making the crossing so far this year by more than 40 percent compared with 2025.

Oops, something went wrong
Oil prices tumbled more than seven percent on Monday, the eve of crucial midterm elections in the United States, as signals that Tehran and Washington were renewing dialogue boosted hopes of ending the Middle East war.
Iran on Monday said "intensive" exchanges were underway with Washington and offered to reopen the Strait of Hormuz under strict conditions, as efforts escalated to avert a return to conflict.
Earlier, the Axios news outlet reported that US Vice President JD Vance had sent a letter to Iranian national security chief Mohsen Rezaei about possible new talks.
That was the highest-level move from President Donald Trump's administration in months.
Again Capital's John Kilduff described investors as experiencing "a violent change in market sentiment," adding that "we went from really, I think, expecting a major offensive after tomorrow's US elections to a potential breakthrough," he told AFP.
"All these losses will be taken right back if this doesn't pan out," Kilduff said.
The steep drop in oil prices translated into weakness among petroleum stocks. But Wall Street shares otherwise began the day with promise, bouncing back after last Friday's rout precipitated by worries over the tech industry's massive artificial intelligence spending.
But tech shares came under pressure as the session progressed, with the tech-focused Nasdaq slumping 1.1 percent.
"This is still a market that is on edge," said Joseph Zidle, chief market strategist at Cresset Capital, who described unease about midterm elections as adding to worries about the AI boom.
"The two of them are actually related," Zidle said of midterms and AI, noting that opposition to data centers has animated many campaigns.
AI has been "on the ballot in so many places, both blue and red," Zidle said. "It seems like data centers are part of the kitchen table issues."
Pollsters expect Democrats to win back control of the House of Representatives, but view Trump's Republican party as potentially able to maintain a majority in the Senate.
The loss of total Republican dominance would push the president into unfamiliar and uncomfortable territory: a lame duck period beset with high inflation at home, the sputtering war against Iran and hostile Democratic investigations into his activities in Washington.
"Investors are bracing for a fresh round of turbulence ahead of US midterm election fireworks while they assess the extent that companies are burning through cash to keep the AI bonfires burning," said Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at Wealth Club.
Earnings this week will come from Apple, which reports after the close of trading on Monday, as well as Advanced Micro Devices and software titan Palantir will be closely watched this week. Shares in Apple fell 1.8 percent.

articles.title_orig: China expands swap and relending tools to steady the stock market
articles.title_zh: China expands swap and relending tools to steady the stock market
articles.content_orig:
China's central bank said it will run swap operations for brokers, fund managers and insurers as conditions warrant, pull in more participants, and trim the fees charged for those swaps. Alongside that, it will lower the interest rate on its relending program tied to share repurchases and stake building to 1% from 1.25%, make that facility a standing feature, and press banks to extend more credit through it.
Both tools debuted in October 2024. The relending channel supplies cheap central bank funding that banks use to make loans backing listed companies and major shareholders who are buying back stock or adding to stakes.
According to the securities regulator, the next swap tranche is expected to start shortly, and 31 approved brokerages and fund managers are together applying for quotas exceeding 100 billion yuan, or about $15 billion. The latest tally from the central bank shows swaps outstanding at 105 billion yuan, while roughly 440 billion yuan in loans tied to buybacks and stake-raising have been signed and over 280 billion yuan has already been paid out.
A meeting on the measures drew 23 securities firms and funds and 26 banks. Speakers included representatives from China International Capital Corp., Guotai Haitong Securities Co., Citic Securities Co., Industrial & Commercial Bank of China Ltd., China Construction Bank Corp. and China Citic Bank Corp.
When markets shift, thoughtful tools can help investors find clearer paths forward. We're hosting our first ever investor livestream on 11/17 to show you how to use ChatGPT and Claude to invest like a pro, hosted by Briefs Finance CEO Jaspreet Singh. Save your seat .
The CSRC plans to broaden who can tap the relending program, including encouraging more companies that are major components of key indexes and more leading technology companies to participate. It also plans to ease buyback restrictions, allowing repurchases when shares fall under the IPO price, and mandating that firms holding surplus funds from capital raises carry out buybacks once market-support thresholds are triggered.
The regulator will study adjustments to margin financing - borrowing to buy stocks - to moderately raise financing capacity and help liquidity.
Beijing is leaning into a "slow bull" approach to entice household savings toward equities, but shaky market action has complicated that push, according to Gavekal Dragonomics. "The government wants to be seen as supportive, or investor confidence could decline even further," wrote Thomas Gatley and Xiaoxi Zhang, noting households remain cautious. The CSI 300 dropped 8.5% in October - its worst monthly fall in more than 10 years - and notched an unprecedented 12-week losing streak ending Friday.
In plain English: cheaper, permanent relending, more participants in the swap tool, looser buyback allowances and potential tweaks to margin financing all target one thing - steadier liquidity and incremental support for shares. Watch how quickly the coming swap tranche is allocated and how broad the relending coverage becomes, since the scale and speed will shape how much lift reaches Chinese equities.

articles.title_orig: U.S., Russia and Ukraine to resume peace talks in Abu Dhabi next week, Witkoff says
articles.title_zh: U.S., Russia and Ukraine to resume peace talks in Abu Dhabi next week, Witkoff says
articles.content_orig:
Volodymyr Zelenskyy says attack in Komyshuvakha was ‘vile’ and shows Russia does not want to de-escalate
Russia on Monday bombed an aid distribution centre and neighbouring shelter in southern Ukraine , killing at least 26 ​people, Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy and the country’s emergency services said.
Emergency services said two members of a rescue crew and four police officers were among the dead in the village ⁠of Komyshuvakha, in south-eastern Zaporizhzhia region. Five people were being treated in hospital, including two rescue workers.
Zelenskyy, in his nightly video address, said Russian forces initially dropped bombs on a school in the village that was used as a shelter and for ⁠distributing humanitarian assistance.
There were no classes at the school, he said, as the village, lying south-east of the region’s main city, ​also called Zaporizhzhia, was too close to the frontline. ‌
“The Russians struck first ‌just as people were arriving – a few aerial bombs,” he said. “Then there was a second strike – more air bombs, this time on ‌the shelter. A vile terrorist strike.”
As night fell in Komyshuvakha, emergency responders used torches to search through the rubble of collapsed buildings, according to photos and video posted online by local officials. Regina Kharchenko, secretary of the Zaporizhzhia city council, said that 27 people were missing in the attack.
Efforts to rescue people Monday evening were hindered as Russian drones launched additional attacks in the area that had been bombed, according to Mykhailo Semikin, a military official in Zaporizhzhia.
Zelenskyy said the Russians could not have been unaware that residents remaining in Komyshuvakha gathered each week to pick up humanitarian packages from the site.
The attack, he said, had shown that Moscow was intent on killing people instead of building on the past week’s ceasefire in the embattled southern city of Oleshky , brokered by US first lady Melania Trump.
“Russians continue to demonstrate, time and again, their hatred of Ukraine and everything that exists here,” he said.
“If Russia genuinely ‌wanted de-escalation, there was an opportunity following the situation in Oleshky to continue taking humanitarian steps. We proposed this. But Russia continues to kill people.”
The ceasefire last week enabled an evacuation of the Russian-occupied Oleshky.
It was the longest pause in fighting between the neighbours in the war, now in its fifth year, which has killed hundreds of thousands of people and displaced millions.
The Kremlin said that no other similar missions were being planned “at the moment”.
US-led talks between Russia and Ukraine are set to resume next week, US special envoy Steve Witkoff said on Monday.
President Donald Trump has pushed for a settlement to the dragging war but there has been no breakthrough.
The talks – to be held 10 November and 11 in Abu Dhabi, Witkoff said – come as Kyiv and its European allies worry that Trump has increasingly sided with Moscow.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia’s Huang Gave Blessing to Marvell-Lumentum Megadeal
articles.title_zh: Nvidia’s Huang Gave Blessing to Marvell-Lumentum Megadeal
articles.content_orig:
Marvell Technology 's deal for optical components maker Lumentum will create an "enormous" opportunity to address growing connectivity demands from the artificial intelligence infrastructure buildout, Lumentum CEO Michael Hurlston told CNBC on Monday.
"You need scale-up technology that needs semiconductors and optical working seamlessly together," Marvell CEO Matt Murphy told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street." "We are going to create a new category of company here."
Since the tie-up is a fixed-ratio deal with no cash, the value will depend on the price of Marvell shares. The company said the transaction has an implied enterprise value of $115 billion for Lumentum, in a release.
Marvell shares slumped 13% in trading Monday, while Lumentum's stock sank nearly 19%. But both stocks have been huge winners in the artificial intelligence boom, with Marvell more than doubling in the past year, prior to Monday's sell-off, and Lumentum quadrupling over that stretch.
Through the acquisition, Marvell said it can combine electrical and optical technologies to meet accelerating and shifting AI connectivity demands across regions and systems. Companies are increasingly relying on optical connections to piece together chips used to run and train large language models.
"We're actually going to create solutions around those that are highly sticky, and the reason that they're sold out is because the demand is exploding, and we don't see that changing anytime soon," Murphy said.
Lumentum shareholders will receive 4.5 Marvell shares for each Lumentum share under the agreement. The deal is expected to close during the first half of 2028.
Marvell's takeover marks one of the most significant bets on AI in 2026 and comes despite recent concerns over the long-term sustainability of infrastructure spending.
This isn't the company's first bet on AI growth. This year, the company closed a multibillion-dollar deal for Celestial AI, a startup focused on optical interconnectivity technology.
Marvell 's Murphy also shot down concerns about Nvidia's circular dealmaking, given the leading AI chipmaker's recent multibillion-dollar investments in both companies.
In a bid to further support the data center infrastructure that houses its AI chips, Nvidia has positioned itself as a central cog in a network of related companies, investing in several technology companies that purchase its chips or neoclouds that rent out computing capacity. That's sparked criticism that companies like Nvidia are virtually funding themselves by taking stakes in customers.
"This is a double down on supporting Nvidia, who is the ecosystem leader in this area," Murphy told CNBC. "We're very committed to that partnership, and I think having two of the key suppliers come together, that support that ecosystem, is going to be a big benefit for them."
Marvell has seen its market value more than triple over the last three years, buoyed by unrelenting AI enthusiasm. Lumentum's stock has more than doubled in 2026 alone.
CORRECTION: This story has been updated to reflect that Lumentum CEO Michael Hurlston described the deal as an 'enormous' opportunity. A previous version of this story incorrectly cited the Marvell CEO.

articles.title_orig: Trump to remove Rwanda and South Africa from US trade deal
articles.title_zh: Trump to remove Rwanda and South Africa from US trade deal
articles.content_orig:
Last year, Trump accused South Africa of white genocide in a meeting with President Cyril Ramaphosa at the White House
US President Donald Trump has notified Congress of his intention to remove South Africa and Rwanda from a preferential trade programme, from 1 January 2027.
The African Growth and Opportunity Act (Agoa) allows eligible African countries to export thousands of products to the US duty-free.
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said in a statement that an annual review had found that both countries were engaging in practices inconsistent with the programme's eligibility requirements.
He added that the Trump administration had additionally notified the two countries of the decision.
The Trump administration cited barriers to US trade and investment, as well as concerns over national security and foreign policy interests in the region.
For South Africa, the US pointed to corruption.
"The Trump administration is working to ensure our African partners take the necessary steps to meet the eligibility criteria," Greer said.
South Africa's Trade Minister Parks Tau described the decision as "unfortunate", saying Washington was raising new issues that had not featured in trade negotiations between the two countries, which began in 2025.
"We will continue to accelerate the diversification of South Africa's export markets to protect jobs," Tau said.
US Ambassador to South Africa Leo Brent Bozell III said it was regrettable that South African policies led to its termination from Agoa.
"This was a predictable and preventable outcome resulting from the rejection by South Africa's government of real concerns raised by the US," he wrote on X.
The announcement comes amid strained relations between Washington and both countries, with the proposed termination threatening their access to preferential trade arrangements with the US.
Last year, Trump accused South Africa of persecuting its white minority and launched a programme for white Afrikaners to get asylum in the US.
Trump also repeated widely discredited claims of a genocide of South Africa's white population.

In Rwanda's case, Washington also raised concerns about human rights, political pluralism, the rule of law and workers' rights.
The move comes barely a week after Rwanda's defence ministry was hit with sanctions by US Treasury for its alleged role in the armed rebellion in eastern DR Congo .
The US Treasury said Rwanda's defence ministry directed thousands of troops to fight alongside M23 rebels in eastern DR Congo, providing weapons, equipment, logistics and training.
Rwanda has denied backing the M23 despite overwhelming evidence.

articles.title_orig: How To Quit Spotify And Improve Your Life In The Process
articles.title_zh: How To Quit Spotify And Improve Your Life In The Process
articles.content_orig:
It's a lot easier than you're probably thinking
Having already been in the news over the past few years for not paying artists, laying off its own workforce and supporting the genocide in Palestine , Spotify was once again in the news this week for shitty reasons, specifically that the company is about to roll out a ghoulish AI-powered remix/cover feature .
The best time and reason to ditch Spotify was when any of that other stuff came to light. The second-best time is today , so in the spirit of telling this company to get in the bin here's a guide to getting off Spotify and, more importantly, getting your music somewhere else.
1) Choose which competitor you'd like to use instead. If you want to stop streaming altogether, buying albums directly off Bandcamp is a great way to support an artist directly. If you can't shake your dependency on streaming catalogues, there are plenty of alternatives like Tidal, Apple Music and Qobuz. I would not recommend Amazon or YouTube Music for both obvious (both companies suck) and technical reasons (they're bad apps, and YT Music has terrible sound quality).
2) If your new service supports it directly (Apple Music on iOS does, for example), you can sometimes just transfer your Spotify library straight over. If it doesn't, you can use a service like Free Your Music or TuneMyMusic , which might cost you a few bucks but in the grand scheme of things is worth the investment. Those tools will do their best (and by experience they're very good) at moving your whole library, playlists and all, off Spotify and over to your new platform of choice. If you also listened to podcasts within Spotify, most rivals will also offer podcasts within their music app, but if they don't--Android users can't use Apple Podcasts, for example--Pocket Casts is a totally workable solution.
3) Once your library has transferred, delete your Spotify account, then block their email addresses, because after a few weeks they'll start sending you pathetic offers like this:
4) That's it. What, were you expecting some long, drawn-out, 2000-word guide? It's extremely easy to get off Spotify while keeping your library intact, and you don't owe that company shit. What are you waiting for.
